title: Part 2, Chapter 48
paragraphs: About what happened to Don Quixote with Doña Rodriguez, the duchess's duenna, together with other occurrences worthy of record and eternal remembrance

Exceedingly moody and dejected was the sorely wounded Don Quixote, his face bandaged and marked — not by the hand of God but by the claws of a cat, the kind of mishap that comes with the territory of knight-errantry.

For six days he stayed out of sight, and one night as he lay awake brooding over his misfortunes and over Altisidora's pursuit of him, he noticed someone unlocking the door of his room with a key. At once he made up his mind that the lovestruck damsel was coming to assault his chastity and put him at risk of failing in the loyalty he owed his lady Dulcinea del Toboso. "No," he said, fully persuaded of the truth of his guess (and loud enough to be heard), "the greatest beauty on earth shall not make me renounce my adoration of her whom I carry stamped and engraved in the core of my heart and the secret depths of my being. Be you, my lady, transformed into a clumsy country wench, or into a nymph of the golden Tagus weaving a web of silk and gold, let Merlin or Montesinos hold you captive where they will — wherever you are, you are mine, and wherever I am, I must be yours." The instant he had finished saying this, the door opened. He stood up on the bed, wrapped head to foot in a yellow satin coverlet, a cap on his head, and his face and moustaches tied up — his face because of the scratches, and his moustaches to keep them from drooping. In this getup he looked the most extraordinary scarecrow imaginable. He kept his eyes fixed on the door, and just as he was expecting the lovesick Altisidora to appear, in came a most venerable duenna in a long white-bordered veil that covered her head to foot. Between the fingers of her left hand she held a short lit candle, while with her right she shaded it to keep the light out of her eyes, which were hidden behind enormous spectacles, and she crept forward in noiseless steps, treading very softly.

Don Quixote watched her from his watchtower, and noting her costume and her silence concluded that this must be some witch or sorceress come in such disguise to work him some mischief, and he began crossing himself at a furious rate. The apparition kept advancing, and on reaching the middle of the room looked up and saw the energy with which Don Quixote was crossing himself. If he had been scared by the look of her, she was terrified at the sight of him — for the moment she saw his tall yellow form with the coverlet and the bandages that disfigured him, she let out a loud scream, exclaimed, "Jesus! What's this I'm seeing?" and dropped the candle in her fright. Then, finding herself in the dark, she turned to flee, but stumbled on her skirts in her panic and went sprawling full length to the floor.

Don Quixote in his alarm began saying, "I conjure you, phantom, or whatever you are, tell me what you are and what you want of me. If you are a soul in torment, say so, and I will do everything in my power for you, for I am a Catholic Christian and love to do good to all the world; and to that end I have embraced the order of knight-errantry to which I belong, whose remit extends even to doing good to souls in purgatory."

The wretched duenna, hearing herself conjured this way, guessed Don Quixote's fear from her own and answered in a low plaintive voice, "Señor Don Quixote — if you really are Don Quixote — I am no phantom or spectre or soul in purgatory, as you seem to think, but Doña Rodriguez, duenna of honour to my lady the duchess, and I come to you with one of those grievances your worship is in the habit of redressing."

"Tell me, Señora Doña Rodriguez," said Don Quixote, "do you perhaps come to transact any go-between business? Because I must tell you I am not available for anybody's purposes, thanks to the peerless beauty of my lady Dulcinea del Toboso. In short, Señora Doña Rodriguez, if you will leave out and set aside all love-messages, you may go and light your candle and come back, and we will discuss any commands you have for me and whatever you wish — except, as I said, any seductive communications."

"I carry nobody's messages, señor," said the duenna; "little you know me. I'm not so far gone in years as to take up such childish tricks. God be praised, I still have a soul in my body and all my teeth and grinders in my mouth, except one or two that the colds, so common here in Aragon, have robbed me of. But wait a moment while I go and light my candle, and I'll be back at once to lay my sorrows before you, as before one who relieves those of all the world." And without waiting for an answer she left the room, leaving Don Quixote tranquilly meditating while he waited for her. A thousand thoughts struck him at once on the subject of this new adventure, and it occurred to him that it was ill-done and worse-advised of him to expose himself to the danger of breaking his pledged faith to his lady. He said to himself, "Who knows but that the devil, being cunning and crafty, may be trying now to entrap me with a duenna, having failed with empresses, queens, duchesses, marchionesses, and countesses? Many a time I have heard sensible men say that the devil will sooner offer you a flat-nosed wench than a roman-nosed one; and who knows but this privacy, this opportunity, this silence, may awaken my sleeping desires, and lead me in my latter years to fall where I have never tripped? In cases like this it is better to flee than to wait for the battle. But I must be out of my senses to think and say such nonsense, for it is impossible that a long, white-hooded, spectacled duenna could stir up or excite a wanton thought in the most graceless bosom in the world. Is there a duenna on earth with fair flesh? Is there a duenna in the world who escapes being ill-tempered, wrinkled, and prudish? Be gone, then, you whole duenna crew, you delight in nobody. Oh, but that lady did well who, they say, kept at the end of her reception room a pair of figures of duennas with spectacles and lace-cushions, as if at work — and those statues served just as well to give the room an air of propriety as if they had been real duennas."

So saying he leapt off the bed, meaning to shut the door and not let Señora Rodriguez in. But just as he was going to close it, Señora Rodriguez returned with her wax candle lit, and getting a closer view of Don Quixote with the coverlet around him, his bandages and his night-cap, she was alarmed all over again, retreated a couple of paces, and exclaimed, "Am I safe, sir knight? Because I don't take it as a very great sign of virtue that your worship should have got out of bed."
"I may well ask the same, señora," said Don Quixote; "and I do ask — shall I be safe from being assailed and forced?"
"Of whom and against whom do you demand that security, sir knight?" said the duenna.

"Of you and against you I ask it," said Don Quixote; "for I am not marble, nor are you brass; it is not now ten o'clock in the morning but midnight, or a little past, I think; and we are in a room more secluded and retired than the cave can have been where the treacherous and daring Aeneas enjoyed the fair soft-hearted Dido. But give me your hand, señora — I require no better protection than my own continence and sense of propriety, plus what is inspired by that venerable head-dress." And so saying he kissed her right hand and took it in his own, she yielding it with equal ceremony. And here Cide Hamete inserts a parenthesis in which he says that to have seen the pair walking from the door to the bed, linked hand in hand like this, he would have given the better of the two tunics he had.

Don Quixote at last got into bed, and Doña Rodriguez sat down on a chair some little distance from his couch, without taking off her spectacles or setting aside the candle. Don Quixote wrapped the bedclothes round him and covered himself completely, leaving nothing but his face visible, and as soon as both had collected themselves he broke the silence, saying, "Now, Señora Doña Rodriguez, you may unburden yourself and pour out everything you have in your sorrowful heart and afflicted bowels; and by me you shall be listened to with chaste ears, and aided by compassionate action."

"I believe it," replied the duenna; "from your worship's gentle and winning presence only such a Christian answer could be expected. The fact is, then, Señor Don Quixote, that though you see me seated in this chair, here in the middle of the kingdom of Aragon, and dressed as a despised outcast duenna, I come from the Asturias of Oviedo, of a family connected by blood with many of the best in the province. But my unfortunate luck and the improvidence of my parents — who, somehow, were reduced to poverty before their time — brought me to the court at Madrid, where, for security and to avoid worse misfortunes, my parents placed me as seamstress in the service of a lady of quality; and I'd have you know that for hemming and sewing I have never been surpassed by anyone in my life. My parents left me in service and went back to their own country, and a few years later passed on, no doubt, to heaven, for they were excellent good Catholic Christians. I was left an orphan with nothing but the miserable wages and trifling presents given to servants of my kind in palaces. About this time, without any encouragement on my part, one of the esquires of the household fell in love with me — a man somewhat advanced in years, full-bearded and presentable, and above all as good a gentleman as the king himself, since he came of mountain stock. Our love affair was not so secret that it didn't come to the knowledge of my lady, and she, to avoid any fuss, had us married with the full sanction of the holy mother Roman Catholic Church. Of that marriage a daughter was born — to put an end to my good fortune, if I had any. Not that I died in childbirth: I came through it safely and in due season; but shortly afterwards my husband died of a certain shock he received, and if I had time to tell you about it I know your worship would be surprised." And here she began to weep bitterly and said, "Pardon me, Señor Don Quixote, if I cannot control myself, for every time I think of my unfortunate husband my eyes fill up. God bless me — what an air of dignity he used to cut, carrying my lady behind him on a stout mule as black as jet! For in those days they didn't use coaches or chairs as they now say they do, and ladies rode behind their squires. I cannot help telling you this much at least, so that you may notice my worthy husband's good breeding and punctiliousness. As he was turning into the Calle de Santiago in Madrid, which is rather narrow, one of the alcaldes of the Court was coming out of it with two alguacils ahead of him, and as soon as my good squire saw him he wheeled his mule about as if to turn and accompany him. My lady, who was riding behind him, said in a low voice, 'What are you about, you sneak — don't you see that I'm here?' The alcalde, like a polite man, reined in his horse and said, 'Carry on, señor; it is I, rather, who ought to accompany my lady Doña Casilda' — for that was my mistress's name. Still my husband, cap in hand, persisted in trying to accompany the alcalde, and seeing this my lady, filled with rage and vexation, pulled out a big pin — or, I rather think, a bodkin — out of her needle-case and drove it into his back so hard that my husband let out a loud yell and fell writhing to the ground with his lady. Her two lackeys ran to lift her up, and the alcalde and the alguacils did the same; the Guadalajara gate was all in commotion — I mean the idlers gathered there. My mistress came back on foot, and my husband hurried off to a barber's shop swearing he was run right through the guts. My husband's courtesy got such a reputation that the boys gave him no peace in the street; and on that account, and because he was somewhat shortsighted, my lady dismissed him; and it was chagrin at this, I am certain beyond any doubt, that brought on his death. I was left a helpless widow with a daughter on my hands growing up in beauty like the sea-foam. At length, however, since I had the reputation of being an excellent needlewoman, my lady the duchess, then newly married to my lord the duke, offered to take me with her to this kingdom of Aragon, and my daughter too. Here, as time went by, my daughter grew up and with her all the graces in the world: she sings like a lark, dances as quick as thought, foots it like a gipsy, reads and writes like a schoolmaster, and does sums like a miser. Of her neatness I say nothing, for running water is not purer; and her age now, if my memory serves me, is sixteen years, five months, and three days, one more or less. To come to the point: the son of a very rich farmer, living in a village of my lord the duke's not very far from here, fell in love with this girl of mine; and in short, how I don't know, they came together, and under the promise of marrying her he made a fool of my daughter, and will not keep his word. And though my lord the duke is aware of it (for I have complained to him, not once but many and many a time, and begged him to order the farmer to marry my daughter), he turns a deaf ear and will scarcely listen to me — the reason being that the seducer's father is so rich, and lends him money, and is constantly going surety for his debts, that he does not want to offend or annoy him in any way. Now, señor, I want your worship to take it upon yourself to redress this wrong, either by entreaty or by arms, for by what all the world says you came into it to redress grievances and right wrongs and help the unfortunate. Let your worship consider the unprotected condition of my daughter, her youth, and all the perfections I have said she possesses; and before God and on my conscience, out of all the damsels my lady has, there is not one who comes up to the sole of her shoe; and the one they call Altisidora, who is reckoned the boldest and gayest of them, doesn't come within two leagues of my daughter. For I would have you know, señor, that all is not gold that glitters, and that same little Altisidora has more forwardness than good looks and more impudence than modesty — besides being not very sound, for she has such a disagreeable breath that one cannot bear to be near her for a moment; and even my lady the duchess — but I'll hold my tongue, for they say walls have ears."
"For heaven's sake, Doña Rodriguez, what ails my lady the duchess?" asked Don Quixote.

"Adjured like that," replied the duenna, "I cannot help answering the question and telling the whole truth. Señor Don Quixote, have you noticed the comeliness of my lady the duchess — that smooth complexion of hers like a burnished polished sword, those two cheeks of milk and carmine, that gay lively step with which she treads, or rather seems to spurn the earth, so that one would think she went radiating health wherever she passed? Well then, let me tell you, she may thank, first of all, God, for it, and next two issues she has, one in each leg, by which all the bad humours, of which the doctors say she is full, are discharged."

"Blessed Virgin!" exclaimed Don Quixote; "and is it possible that my lady the duchess has drains of that sort? I wouldn't have believed it if the barefoot friars had told me; but since the lady Doña Rodriguez says so, it must be so. But surely such issues, and in such places, do not discharge humours but liquid amber. Truly, I do believe now that this practice of opening issues is a very important matter for the health."

Don Quixote had hardly said this when the chamber door flew open with a loud bang, and the noise so startled Doña Rodriguez that she let the candle fall from her hand, and the room was left as dark as a wolf's mouth, as the saying is. Suddenly the poor duenna felt two hands seize her by the throat, so tightly that she could not croak, while someone else, without saying a word, very briskly hoisted up her petticoats, and with what seemed to be a slipper began to lay on so heartily that anyone would have felt pity for her. But although Don Quixote felt sorry for her, he never stirred from his bed; he lay quiet and silent, fearing that his turn for a drubbing might be coming. Nor was the fear groundless: leaving the duenna (who did not dare cry out) well basted, the silent executioners fell upon Don Quixote, stripped him of the sheet and the coverlet, and pinched him so fast and so hard that he was driven to defend himself with his fists — all of it in marvellous silence. The battle lasted nearly half an hour, and then the phantoms fled. Doña Rodriguez gathered up her skirts, and bemoaning her fate went out without a word to Don Quixote, and he, sorely pinched, puzzled, and dejected, was left alone — and there we will leave him, wondering who could have been the perverse enchanter who had reduced him to such a state. But that shall be told in due season, for Sancho claims our attention, and the orderly arrangement of the story demands it.

title: Part 2, Chapter 49
paragraphs: About what happened to Sancho on the round of his island

We left the great governor angered and irritated by that portrait-painting rogue of a farmer who, coached by the majordomo (as the majordomo had been by the duke), tried to play him for a fool. But fool, boor, and clown though he was, Sancho held his own against them all, saying to those around him and to Doctor Pedro Recio — who, once the private business of the duke's letter was settled, had returned to the room — "Now I see plainly enough that judges and governors must be made of brass not to feel the pestering of the petitioners who at all times and in all seasons insist on being heard, and having their business dispatched, and their own affairs and no others attended to, come what may. And if the poor judge doesn't hear them and settle the matter — either because he can't or because that's not the time he has set aside for hearing them — they instantly abuse him, run him down, gnaw at his bones, and even pick holes in his pedigree. You silly, stupid petitioner, don't be in a hurry; wait for the proper time and season for doing business; don't come at dinner-hour or bedtime, for judges are only flesh and blood and must give Nature what she naturally demands of them — all except myself, for in my case I give her nothing to eat, thanks to Señor Doctor Pedro Recio Tirteafuera here, who would have me die of hunger, and declares that death to be life; and the same sort of life may God give him and all his kind — I mean the bad doctors, for the good ones deserve palms and laurels."

Everyone who knew Sancho Panza was astonished to hear him speak so elegantly, and they couldn't account for it except by supposing that office and grave responsibility either sharpen or stupefy a man's wits. At last Doctor Pedro Recio Agilers of Tirteafuera promised to let him have supper that night, even if it broke every aphorism of Hippocrates. With that the governor was satisfied, and he looked forward to the approach of night and supper-time with great anxiety; and though time, to his mind, stood still and made no progress, still the hour he so longed for came, and they gave him a beef salad with onions and some boiled calves' feet rather far gone. At this he fell to with greater relish than if they'd given him francolins from Milan, pheasants from Rome, veal from Sorrento, partridges from Moron, or geese from Lavajos; and turning to the doctor at supper he said, "Look here, señor doctor, in future don't bother trying to give me dainty things or choice dishes to eat — it'll only take my stomach off its hinges. It's used to goat, cow, bacon, hung beef, turnips and onions; and if it gets these palace dishes by any chance, it receives them squeamishly, and sometimes with disgust. What the head-carver should do is serve me with what they call _ollas podridas_ (and the rottener they are the better they smell); and he can put whatever he likes into them, so long as it's good to eat, and I'll be grateful to him and pay him back some day. But let nobody play pranks on me, for either we are or we are not. Let's live and eat in peace and good fellowship, for when God sends the dawn, he sends it for all. I mean to govern this island without giving up a right or taking a bribe; let everyone keep his eye open, and look out for the arrow; for I can tell them 'the devil's in Cantillana,' and if they drive me to it they'll see something that will astonish them. No — make yourself honey and the flies will eat you."

"Truly, señor governor," said the carver, "your worship is in the right of it in everything you have said; and I promise you in the name of all the inhabitants of this island that they will serve your worship with all zeal, affection, and goodwill, for the mild kind of government you've shown a sample of to begin with leaves them no ground for doing or thinking anything to your worship's disadvantage."

"That I believe," said Sancho; "and they would be great fools if they did or thought otherwise. Once more I say: see to my feeding and my Dapple's, for that's the great point and what is most to the purpose; and when the hour comes, let's go the rounds, for it's my intention to purge this island of all manner of uncleanness and of all idle good-for-nothing vagabonds; for I would have you know that lazy idlers are the same thing in a state as drones in a hive, eating up the honey the industrious bees make. I mean to protect the husbandman, preserve the gentleman his privileges, reward the virtuous, and above all respect religion and honour its ministers. What do you say to that, my friends? Is there anything in what I say, or am I talking to no purpose?"

"There is so much in what your worship says, señor governor," said the majordomo, "that I am filled with wonder to see a man like your worship, entirely without learning (for I believe you have none at all), say such things, so full of sound maxims and sage remarks, very different from what was expected of your worship's intelligence by those who sent us, or by us who came here. Every day we see something new in this world: jokes turn into realities, and the jokers find the tables turned upon them."

Night came, and with Doctor Pedro Recio's permission the governor had supper. They then got ready to go the rounds, and he started out with the majordomo, the secretary, the head-carver, the chronicler charged with recording his deeds, and alguacils and notaries enough to form a fair-sized squadron. In the middle marched Sancho with his staff, as fine a sight as one could wish to see; and only a few streets of the town had been covered when they heard a noise as of clashing swords. They hurried to the spot and found the combatants were only two, who on seeing the authorities approaching stood still, one of them exclaiming, "Help, in the name of God and the king! Are men to be allowed to rob in the middle of this town, and rush out and attack people in the very streets?"
"Calm down, my good man," said Sancho, "and tell me what is the cause of this quarrel; for I am the governor."

Said the other combatant, "Señor governor, I will tell you in very few words. Your worship must know that this gentleman has just now won more than a thousand reals in the gambling house opposite, and God knows how. I was there, and gave more than one doubtful point in his favour, very much against what my conscience told me. He made off with his winnings, and when I was sure he was going to give me a crown or so at least by way of a tip — as is usual and customary to give men of quality of my sort, who stand by to see fair or foul play, and back up swindles, and prevent quarrels — he pocketed his money and left the house. Indignant at this I followed him, and speaking to him fairly and civilly asked him to give me, if it were only eight reals; for he knows I am an honest man and that I have neither profession nor property, my parents never having brought me up to any or left me any. But the rogue, who is a greater thief than Cacus and a greater sharper than Andradilla, would not give me more than four reals; so your worship can see how little shame and conscience he has. But by my faith, if you had not come up, I'd have made him disgorge his winnings, and he'd have learned what the range of the steelyard was."

"What do you say to this?" asked Sancho. The other replied that everything his antagonist said was true, and that he did not choose to give him more than four reals because he very often gave him money already; and that those who expect tips ought to be civil and take what is given them with a cheerful face, and not make any claim against winners unless they know them for certain to be sharpers and their winnings unfairly won; and that there could be no better proof of his own honesty than his having refused to give anything, for sharpers always pay tribute to lookers-on who know them.
"That's true," said the majordomo. "Let your worship consider what is to be done with these men."

"What is to be done," said Sancho, "is this: you, the winner, be you good, bad, or indifferent, give this opponent of yours a hundred reals at once, and you must hand over thirty more for the poor prisoners; and you, who have neither profession nor property and hang about the island in idleness, take these hundred reals now, and some time tomorrow quit the island under sentence of banishment for ten years, under pain of completing it in another life if you violate the sentence — for I'll hang you on a gibbet, or at least the hangman will by my orders. Not a word from either of you, or I'll make him feel my hand."

The one paid down the money and the other took it, and the latter quit the island while the former went home; and then the governor said, "Either I am not good for much, or I'll get rid of these gambling houses, for it strikes me they are very mischievous."

"This one at least," said one of the notaries, "your worship will not be able to get rid of, for a great man owns it, and what he loses each year is beyond all comparison more than what he makes at the cards. On the minor gambling houses your worship can exercise your power, and it's those that do the most harm and shelter the most barefaced practices. In the houses of lords and gentlemen of quality, the notorious sharpers don't dare try their tricks; and since the vice of gambling has become so common, it is better that men should play in houses of repute than in some tradesman's, where they catch an unlucky fellow in the small hours of the morning and skin him alive."
"I already know, notary, that there's a good deal to be said on that point," said Sancho.

And now a tipstaff came up with a young man in his grasp and said, "Señor governor, this youth was coming towards us, and as soon as he saw the officers of justice he turned about and ran like a deer — a sure proof that he must be some evildoer. I ran after him, and if it hadn't been for his stumbling and falling, I'd never have caught him."
"What did you run for, fellow?" said Sancho.
To which the young man replied, "Señor, it was to avoid answering all the questions officers of justice ask."
"What's your trade?"
"A weaver."
"And what do you weave?"
"Lance heads, with your worship's good leave."
"Being facetious with me, are you? You pride yourself on being a wag? Very good — and where were you going just now?"
"To take the air, señor."
"And where does one take the air on this island?"
"Where it blows."

"Good — your answers are very much to the point; you're a smart youth. But take notice that I am the air, and that I blow upon you a-stern, and send you to gaol. Ho there! Lay hold of him and take him off; I'll make him sleep there tonight without air."
"By God," said the young man, "your worship will make me sleep in gaol just as soon as you'll make me king."
"Why shan't I make you sleep in gaol?" said Sancho. "Don't I have the power to arrest you and release you whenever I like?"
"For all the power your worship has," said the young man, "you won't be able to make me sleep in gaol."

"How — not able?" said Sancho. "Take him away at once where he'll see his mistake with his own eyes, even if the gaoler is willing to exert his interested generosity on his behalf; for I'll lay a penalty of two thousand ducats on the gaoler if he allows him to stir a step from the prison."
"That's ridiculous," said the young man; "the fact is, all the men on earth will not make me sleep in prison."
"Tell me, you devil," said Sancho, "do you have some angel who will deliver you and take off the irons I am about to order them to put on you?"

"Now, señor governor," said the young man in a sprightly manner, "let's be reasonable and come to the point. Granted that your worship may order me to be taken to prison, and have irons and chains put on me, and be shut up in a cell, and may lay heavy penalties on the gaoler if he lets me out, and that he obeys your orders — still, if I don't choose to sleep, and choose to remain awake all night without closing an eye, will your worship with all your power be able to make me sleep if I don't choose?"
"No, truly," said the secretary, "and the fellow has made his point."
"So then," said Sancho, "it would be entirely by your own choice that you would keep from sleeping — not in opposition to my will?"
"No, señor," said the youth, "certainly not."

"Well then, go, and God be with you," said Sancho. "Be off home to sleep, and God give you sound sleep, for I don't want to rob you of it; but in future, let me advise you, don't joke with the authorities, because you may come across someone who will bring down the joke on your own skull."

The young man went on his way, and the governor continued his round; and shortly afterwards two tipstaffs came up with a person in custody and said, "Señor governor, this person, who appears to be a man, is not so, but a woman — and not an ill-looking one — in man's clothes." They raised two or three lanterns to her face, and by their light made out the features of a woman to all appearance about sixteen or a little older, with her hair gathered into a gold and green silk net, and fair as a thousand pearls. They looked her over from head to foot and noticed she had on red silk stockings with garters of white taffeta bordered with gold and pearl; her breeches were of green and gold stuff, and under an open jacket or jerkin of the same she wore a doublet of the finest white and gold cloth; her shoes were white and of a man's pattern; she carried no sword at her belt, only a richly ornamented dagger, and on her fingers she had several handsome rings. In short, the girl looked beautiful in everyone's eyes, and none of those who beheld her recognised her; the townspeople said they could not imagine who she was; and those who were in on the secret of the jokes that were being played on Sancho were the ones most surprised, for this incident or discovery had not been arranged by them; and they watched anxiously to see how the affair would end.

Sancho was struck by the girl's beauty, and asked her who she was, where she was going, and what had prompted her to dress in that garb. She, with her eyes fixed on the ground, answered in modest confusion, "I cannot tell you, señor, in front of so many people what it is of such consequence to me to have kept secret. One thing I do wish to be known: that I am no thief or evildoer, but only an unhappy maiden whom the power of jealousy has led to break through the respect that is due to modesty."
Hearing this the majordomo said to Sancho, "Make the people stand back, señor governor, so this lady can say what she wants to with less embarrassment."

Sancho gave the order, and all but the majordomo, the head-carver, and the secretary fell back. Finding herself with no more onlookers, the damsel went on to say, "I am the daughter, sirs, of Pedro Perez Mazorca, the wool-farmer of this town, who is in the habit of coming very often to my father's house."

"That won't do, señora," said the majordomo; "for I know Pedro Perez very well, and I know he has no child at all, either son or daughter; and besides, though you say he is your father, you add that he comes very often to your father's house."
"I had already noticed that," said Sancho.
"I am confused just now, sirs," said the damsel, "and I don't know what I'm saying; but the truth is that I am the daughter of Diego de la Llana, whom you must all know."

"Ah, that will do," said the majordomo; "for I know Diego de la Llana, and know that he is a gentleman of position and a rich man, and that he has a son and a daughter, and that since he was left a widower nobody in all this town can claim to have seen his daughter's face — for he keeps her so closely shut up that he won't even give the sun a chance of seeing her; and for all that, report says she is extremely beautiful."

"It is true," said the damsel, "and I am that daughter. Whether report lies or not as to my beauty, you, sirs, will have decided by now, since you've seen me." And with that she began to weep bitterly.

On seeing this the secretary leant over to the head-carver's ear and said in a low voice, "Something serious has no doubt happened to this poor maiden, that she goes wandering from home in such a dress and at such an hour, and one of her rank too." "There can be no doubt about it," returned the carver, "and moreover her tears confirm your suspicion." Sancho gave her the best comfort he could, and entreated her to tell them, without any fear, what had happened to her, for they would all earnestly and by every means in their power try to relieve her.

"The fact is, sirs," said she, "that my father has kept me shut up these ten years, for so long is it since the earth received my mother. Mass is said at home in a sumptuous chapel, and all this time I have seen but the sun in the heaven by day, and the moon and the stars by night; nor do I know what streets are like, or plazas, or churches, or even men, except for my father, a brother I have, and Pedro Perez the wool-farmer; whom, because he came frequently to our house, I took it into my head to call my father, to avoid naming my own. This seclusion and the restrictions laid upon my going out, were it only to church, have kept me unhappy for many a day and month. I longed to see the world, or at least the town where I was born, and it didn't seem to me that this wish was inconsistent with the respect maidens of good quality should have for themselves. When I heard them talking about bull-fights taking place, and about javelin games, and about the staging of plays, I asked my brother — who is a year younger than me — to tell me what these sorts of things were, and many more I had never seen. He explained them to me as well as he could, but the only effect was to kindle in me an even stronger desire to see them. At last, to cut short the story of my ruin, I begged and entreated my brother — oh, that I had never made such an entreaty —" And once more she gave way to a burst of weeping.
"Carry on, señora," said the majordomo, "and finish your story of what has happened to you, for your words and tears are keeping us all in suspense."
"I have but little more to say, though many a tear yet to shed," said the damsel; "for ill-placed desires can only be paid for in some such way."

The maiden's beauty had made a deep impression on the head-carver's heart, and he again raised his lantern for another look at her, and thought that what she was shedding were not tears but seed-pearl or dew of the meadow; nay, he exalted them still higher, and made Oriental pearls of them, and fervently hoped her misfortune might not be as great as her tears and sobs seemed to suggest. The governor was losing patience at the length of time the girl was taking to tell her story, and told her not to keep them waiting any longer, for it was late, and there was still a good deal of the town to be gone over.

She, with broken sobs and half-suppressed sighs, went on to say, "My misfortune, my misadventure, is simply this — that I begged my brother to dress me up as a man in a suit of his clothes, and take me out some night, when our father was asleep, to see the whole town. He, won over by my entreaties, consented; and dressing me in this suit, and himself in clothes of mine that fitted him as if made for him (for he has not a hair on his chin, and might pass for a very beautiful young girl), tonight, about an hour ago, more or less, we left the house; and guided by our youthful and foolish impulse we made the circuit of the whole town; and then, as we were about to return home, we saw a great troop of people coming, and my brother said to me, 'Sister, this must be the round; stir your feet and put wings to them, and follow me as fast as you can, in case they recognise us, for that would be a bad business for us.' And so saying he turned about and began — I cannot say to run, but to fly. In less than six paces I fell from fright, and then the officer of justice came up and carried me before your worships, where I find myself put to shame before all these people as whimsical and vicious."
"So then, señora," said Sancho, "no other mishap has befallen you, nor was it jealousy that made you leave home, as you said at the beginning of your story?"
"Nothing has happened to me," said she, "and it wasn't jealousy that brought me out, but merely a longing to see the world, which did not go beyond seeing the streets of this town."

The appearance of the tipstaffs with her brother in custody, whom one of them had caught up with as he ran from his sister, now fully confirmed the truth of what the damsel said. He had on nothing but a rich petticoat and a short blue damask cloak with fine gold lace, and his head was uncovered and adorned only with its own hair, which looked like rings of gold, so bright and curly was it. The governor, the majordomo, and the carver took him aside and, out of his sister's hearing, asked him how he came to be in that dress; and he, with no less shame and embarrassment, told exactly the same story as his sister, to the great delight of the enamoured carver. The governor, however, said to them, "In truth, young lady and gentleman, this has been a very childish affair, and to explain your folly and rashness there was no need for all this delay and all these tears and sighs. If you had said, 'We are so-and-so, and we escaped from our father's house in this way in order to ramble about, out of mere curiosity and with no other object,' there would have been an end of the matter, and none of these little sobs and tears and all the rest of it."
"That is true," said the damsel, "but you see the confusion I was in was so great it didn't let me behave as I should."

"No harm done," said Sancho. "Come, we'll leave you at your father's house; perhaps they will not have missed you; and another time don't be so childish or eager to see the world — for a respectable damsel should have a broken leg and keep at home; and 'the woman and the hen by gadding about are soon lost'; and 'she who is eager to see is also eager to be seen.' I say no more."

The youth thanked the governor for his kind offer to take them home, and they directed their steps towards the house, which was not far off. On reaching it the youth threw a pebble up at a grating, and immediately a maidservant who was waiting for them came down and opened the door, and they went in, leaving the party marvelling as much at their grace and beauty as at the fancy they'd had for seeing the world by night and without leaving the village — which, however, they put down to their youth.

The head-carver was left with a heart pierced through and through, and made up his mind on the spot to ask the damsel's father for her hand in marriage the next morning, sure she would not be refused him as he was a servant of the duke's; and even Sancho found himself entertaining ideas and schemes about marrying the youth to his daughter Sanchica, and resolved to open negotiations at the proper season, persuading himself that no husband could be refused to a governor's daughter. And so the night's round came to an end — and the government a couple of days later, whereby all his plans were overthrown and swept away, as will be seen further on.

title: Part 2, Chapter 50
paragraphs: Which reveals who the enchanters and executioners were that flogged the duenna and pinched Don Quixote, and tells what happened to the page who carried the letter to Teresa Panza, Sancho Panza’s wife

Cide Hamete, that painstaking investigator of every fine detail of this truthful history, reports that when Doña Rodriguez left her own room to go to Don Quixote’s, another duenna who shared her quarters noticed her go; and since all duennas love to pry, eavesdrop, and sniff things out, she followed so quietly that the good Rodriguez never realized it. The moment this duenna saw her enter Don Quixote’s room, true to the duenna’s unfailing custom of carrying tales, she rushed off that very instant to inform the duchess that Doña Rodriguez was shut up alone with Don Quixote. The duchess told the duke and asked his leave for herself and Altisidora to go and discover what that duenna wanted with Don Quixote. The duke agreed, and the two of them crept softly and cautiously to the door of the room and stationed themselves so close to it that they could hear everything said inside. But when the duchess heard how the Rodriguez had made public the Aranjuez of her issues, she could not contain herself, and neither could Altisidora; and so, boiling with rage and thirsting for revenge, they burst into the room, tormented Don Quixote, and flogged the duenna in the manner already described—for insults aimed at their beauty and their vanity rouse the anger of women like nothing else and set them burning for vengeance. The duchess told the duke what had happened, and it amused him greatly; and she, pursuing her scheme of amusing and entertaining herself with Don Quixote, dispatched the page who had played the part of Dulcinea in the negotiations for her disenchantment (which Sancho Panza, absorbed in the cares of governing, had entirely forgotten) to Teresa Panza, his wife, carrying her husband’s letter and another from the duchess herself, together with a great string of fine coral beads as a present.

Now the history tells us this page was sharp and quick-witted, and being eager to please his lord and lady, he set out for Sancho’s village very willingly. Just before entering it he noticed a group of women washing clothes in a brook, and asked them whether they could tell him if there lived in the village a woman named Teresa Panza, wife of one Sancho Panza, squire to a knight called Don Quixote of La Mancha. At the question a young girl who had been washing stood up and said, “Teresa Panza is my mother, and that Sancho is my father, and that knight is our master.”
“Then come along, miss,” said the page, “and show me where your mother is, for I am carrying her a letter and a present from your father.”

“That I’ll do with all my heart, señor,” said the girl, who looked about fourteen, give or take; and leaving the clothes she was washing with one of her companions, without stopping to put anything on her head or her feet—for she was bare-legged and her hair hung loose about her—away she skipped in front of the page’s horse, saying, “Come along, your worship; our house stands at the entrance to the town, and my mother is there, sad enough at heart, for she’s had no news of my father this long, long while.”
“Well,” said the page, “the news I’m bringing her is so good that she’ll have reason to thank God for it.”

And so, skipping, running, and capering, the girl reached the town; but before going into the house she called out from the doorway, “Come out, mother Teresa, come out, come out; here’s a gentleman with letters and other things from my good father.” At these words her mother Teresa Panza came out spinning a bundle of flax, wearing a grey petticoat—so short that it looked as though “they to her shame had cut it short”—a grey bodice of the same cloth, and a smock. She was not very old, though clearly past forty: strong, healthy, sturdy, and browned by the sun. Seeing her daughter, and the page on horseback, she cried, “What’s this, child? Who is this gentleman?”

“A servant of my lady Doña Teresa Panza,” answered the page; and matching the action to the word he flung himself off his horse, went with great humility to kneel before the lady Teresa, and said, “Allow me to kiss your hand, Señora Doña Teresa, as the lawful and only wife of Señor Don Sancho Panza, rightful governor of the island of Barataria.”
“Ah, señor, get up, none of that,” said Teresa; “I’m no court lady at all, only a poor country woman, daughter of a clod-breaker and wife of a squire-errant—not of any governor whatsoever.”

“You are,” said the page, “the most worthy wife of a governor worthy above all others; and in proof of what I say, accept this letter and this present.” With that he drew from his pocket a string of coral beads with gold clasps, set it about her neck, and said, “This letter is from his lordship the governor, and the other, together with these corals, comes from my lady the duchess, who has sent me to your worship.”

Teresa stood dumbfounded, and her daughter no less; and the girl said, “May I die if our master Don Quixote isn’t at the bottom of all this; he must have given father that government or county he promised him so many times.”
“That is the truth,” said the page; “it is thanks to Señor Don Quixote that Señor Sancho is now governor of the island of Barataria, as this letter will show.”
“Would your worship read it to me, noble sir?” said Teresa; “for though I can spin, I can’t read—not a scrap of it.”
“Nor can I,” said Sanchica; “but wait a moment and I’ll go fetch someone who can—the curate himself, or the bachelor Samson Carrasco—and they’ll come gladly to hear any news of my father.”

“There’s no need to fetch anyone,” said the page; “I can’t spin, but I can read, and I’ll read it.” And so he read it through; but since it has already been given, it is not set down here again. He then took out the second letter, the one from the duchess, which ran as follows:

Friend Teresa,—The good qualities of your husband Sancho, of his heart as much as of his head, moved me and indeed obliged me to ask my husband the duke to give him the governorship of one of his many islands. I am told he governs like a gerfalcon, which delights me, and my lord the duke naturally as well; and I thank heaven heartily that I made no mistake in choosing him for that same government—for I would have Señora Teresa understand that a good governor is a rare thing to find in this world, and may God deal as well by me as Sancho governs. I send you with this, my dear, a string of coral beads with gold clasps; I wish they were Oriental pearls, but “he who gives you a bone does not wish you dead.” A day will come when we shall meet and come to know one another—but God alone knows the future. Give my regards to your daughter Sanchica, and tell her from me to hold herself ready, for I mean to marry her high when she least expects it. They tell me the acorns in your village are big ones; send me a couple of dozen or so, and I shall prize them greatly as coming from your hand. Write to me at length, to assure me of your health and well-being; and if you should ever need anything, you have only to open your mouth, and your mouth shall be the measure; and so God keep you.
Written from this place. Your affectionate friend, THE DUCHESS.

“Ah, what a good lady—how plain, how humble!” said Teresa when she had heard the letter. “Let me be buried alongside ladies of that sort, and not the gentlewomen we have in this town, who fancy that because they’re gentlefolk the very wind mustn’t touch them, who go off to church with as many airs as if they were queens, no less, and seem to think themselves disgraced if they so much as look at a farmer’s wife! And see how this good lady, duchess though she is, calls me ‘friend’ and treats me as her equal—and equal may I see her to the tallest church tower in La Mancha! As for the acorns, señor, I’ll send her ladyship a whole peck, and such big ones that folk might come to stare at them as a sight and a wonder. And now, Sanchica, see that the gentleman is made comfortable: put up his horse, fetch some eggs out of the stable, cut plenty of bacon, and let’s give him his dinner like a prince, for the good news he’s brought and that handsome face of his deserve nothing less. Meanwhile I’ll run out and give the neighbours the news of our good luck—and the father curate too, and Master Nicholas the barber, who are and always have been such friends of your father’s.”
“That I’ll do, mother,” said Sanchica; “but mind, you must give me half of that string; for I don’t believe my lady the duchess could have been so foolish as to send the whole of it to you.”
“It’s all for you, my child,” said Teresa; “but let me wear it round my neck for a few days first, for truly it seems to make my heart glad.”

“You’ll be glad too,” said the page, “when you see the bundle inside this portmanteau: a suit of the very finest cloth, which the governor wore only one day out hunting, and now sends, every bit of it, for Señora Sanchica.”
“May he live a thousand years,” said Sanchica, “and the man who brings it just as many—no, two thousand, if need be.”

At this Teresa hurried out of the house with the letters, the string of beads round her neck, drumming on the letters as she went as though they were a tambourine; and chancing to run into the curate and Samson Carrasco, she began capering about and saying, “No poor folk in this family now, faith! We’ve got ourselves a little government! Now let the finest fine lady in town try me, and I’ll put her in her place!”
“What’s all this, Teresa Panza?” they said. “What madness has got into you, and what papers are those?”

“No madness at all,” said she, “except that these are the letters of duchesses and governors, and these things on my neck are fine coral beads, with ave-marias and paternosters of beaten gold—and I am a governess.”
“God help us,” said the curate, “we can’t understand you, Teresa, or make out what you’re talking about.”
“There—you may see it for yourselves,” said Teresa, and she handed them the letters.

The curate read them aloud for Samson Carrasco to hear, and he and Samson stared at one another in astonishment at what they had read; then the bachelor asked who had brought the letters. Teresa answered by inviting them to come with her to her house, where they would see the messenger for themselves—a most elegant young man, who had brought another present worth as much again. The curate lifted the coral beads from her neck and examined them over and over, and once satisfied that they were genuinely fine he fell to marveling all over again, saying, “By the gown I wear, I don’t know what to say or think of these letters and presents. On the one hand I can see and feel how fine these corals are; on the other I read that a duchess writes to beg for a couple of dozen acorns.”
“Make sense of that if you can,” said Carrasco. “Well then, let’s go and see this messenger, and from him we’ll learn something about the mystery that has dropped on us.”

So they did, and Teresa went back with them. They found the page sifting a little barley for his horse, and Sanchica slicing a rasher of bacon to be paved over with eggs for his dinner. His looks and his handsome clothes pleased them both greatly; and after they had greeted him courteously, and he them, Samson asked him to give them his news, of Don Quixote as well as of Sancho Panza—for, he said, though they had read the letters from Sancho and from her ladyship the duchess, they were still bewildered and could not make out what this business of Sancho’s government meant, above all the government of an island, when all or most of the islands in the Mediterranean belonged to his Majesty.

To this the page replied, “That Señor Sancho Panza is a governor admits of no doubt whatever; whether what he governs is an island or not is nothing I concern myself with; it is enough that it’s a town of more than a thousand inhabitants. As to the acorns, I can tell you that my lady the duchess is so plain and unassuming that—never mind sending to beg acorns from a peasant woman—she has been known to send to one of her neighbours to borrow a comb. For I’d have your worships know that the ladies of Aragon, though every bit as illustrious, are not so stiff and haughty as the ladies of Castile; they treat people with far more familiarity.”
In the middle of this conversation Sanchica came in with her skirt full of eggs, and she asked the page, “Tell me, señor, does my father wear trunk-hose now that he’s been made governor?”
“I haven’t noticed,” said the page; “but no doubt he wears them.”
“Ah, my God!” said Sanchica. “What a sight it must be, my father in tights! Isn’t it strange that ever since I was born I’ve had a longing to see my father in trunk-hose?”
“As things are going, you’ll live to see it,” said the page; “by God, if the government only lasts him two months more, he’s well on the way to traveling about under a sunshade.”

The curate and the bachelor could see plainly enough that the page was speaking in jest; but the fineness of the coral beads, and the hunting suit that Sancho had sent (for Teresa had already shown it to them) undid that impression; and they could not help laughing at Sanchica’s wish, still more when Teresa said, “Señor curate, ask about whether anyone here is going to Madrid or Toledo, to buy me a hooped petticoat—a proper fashionable one, of the very best quality—for indeed and indeed I must do honour to my husband’s government as best I can; and if I’m pushed to it and have to, I’ll go to Court and set up a coach like everyone else; for she who has a governor for a husband can very well afford to have one and keep one.”

“And why not, mother!” said Sanchica. “Would to God it were today rather than tomorrow, even if people seeing me sitting in that coach with my mother were to say, ‘Look at that rubbish, that garlic-stuffed fellow’s daughter, how she lolls stretched out at her ease in a coach as if she were a she-pope!’ But let them trudge through the mud while I ride in my coach with my feet off the ground. A bad year to every backbiter in the world; ‘let me go warm and the people may laugh.’ Am I right, mother?”

“Right you are, my child,” said Teresa; “and all this good luck, and even more besides, my good Sancho foretold to me; and you’ll see, my daughter, he won’t stop until he’s made me a countess; for in matters of luck, getting started is everything; and as I’ve heard your good father say many a time—for besides being your father he’s the father of proverbs too—‘When they offer you a heifer, run with the halter; when they offer you a government, take it; when they’d give you a county, seize it; and when they call “Here, here!” with something good, swallow it down.’ Oh certainly—just go on sleeping, and give no answer to the strokes of good fortune and the lucky chances knocking at the door of your house!”
“And what do I care,” Sanchica added, “if somebody seeing me hold my head high says, ‘The dog saw himself in hempen breeches,’ and all the rest of it?”

Hearing this the curate said, “I do believe that everyone in this family of the Panzas is born with a sackful of proverbs inside them; I’ve never seen one of them who doesn’t pour them out at all hours and on every occasion.”

“That is true,” said the page, “for Señor Governor Sancho produces them at every turn; and though a great many of them are beside the point, they give pleasure all the same, and my lady the duchess and the duke praise them to the skies.”

“Then you still maintain, señor,” said the bachelor, “that all this about Sancho’s government is real, and that there actually exists a duchess who sends him presents and writes to him? Because we, even though we’ve handled the present and read the letters, don’t believe it; we suspect it’s something in the style of our fellow townsman Don Quixote, who imagines that everything is done by enchantment; and for that reason I’m almost ready to say I’d like to touch and feel your worship, to find out whether you’re an ambassador of the imagination or a man of flesh and blood.”

“All I know, sirs,” the page answered, “is that I am a real ambassador; that Señor Sancho Panza is governor in actual fact; that my lord and lady the duke and duchess can give—and have given—him that very government; and that I have heard it said Sancho Panza is bearing himself most stoutly in it. Whether there is any enchantment anywhere in all this is a matter for your worships to settle between yourselves; for that is all I know, by the oath I swear—and I swear it on the lives of my parents, who are both still living and whom I love dearly.”
“It may well be so,” said the bachelor; “but _dubitat Augustinus_.”

“Doubt who will,” said the page; “what I’ve told you is the truth, and truth will always rise above falsehood as oil rises above water. If not, _operibus credite, et non verbis_: let one of you come along with me, and his eyes will see what his ears refuse to believe.”
“That trip belongs to me,” said Sanchica; “take me with you, señor, up behind you on your horse; I’ll go with all my heart to see my father.”
“Governors’ daughters,” said the page, “must not travel the roads alone; they go attended by coaches and litters and a great train of servants.”
“By God,” said Sanchica, “I can travel just as well on a she-ass as in a coach. What a dainty little thing you must take me for!”

“Hush, girl,” said Teresa; “you don’t know what you’re saying; the gentleman is quite right, for ‘as the times are, so must the manners be.’ When it was plain Sancho, it was ‘Sancha’; now that it’s governor, it’s ‘señora’—though I don’t know if I’ve put that right.”
“Señora Teresa says more than she knows,” said the page; “and now give me something to eat and send me off at once, for I mean to ride back this very evening.”
“Then come and do penance with me,” said the curate at this; “for Señora Teresa has more goodwill than provisions for serving so worthy a guest.”

The page declined, but in the end had to accept, for his own good; and the curate took him home very gladly, so as to have the chance of questioning him at leisure about Don Quixote and his doings. The bachelor offered to write Teresa’s letters of reply for her; but she had no wish to let him meddle in her affairs, for she thought him rather too fond of a joke; so instead she gave a cake and a couple of eggs to a young acolyte who had a good hand with a pen, and he wrote two letters for her—one for her husband, the other for the duchess—dictated straight out of her own head; and they are not the worst letters set down in this great history, as will be seen further on.

title: Part 2, Chapter 51
paragraphs: How Sancho's government progressed, along with other equally entertaining matters

Day broke after the night of the governor's patrol — a night the head-carver passed without sleeping, so full were his thoughts of the face, the manner, and the beauty of the disguised girl, while the majordomo spent what remained of it writing his lord and lady an account of everything Sancho said and did, as astonished by his sayings as by his doings, for everything about him was a blend of shrewdness and simplicity. The señor governor rose, and on Doctor Pedro Recio's orders they gave him for breakfast a little fruit preserve and four sips of cold water — a meal Sancho would gladly have traded for a piece of bread and a bunch of grapes; but seeing there was no way around it, he submitted, with no small sorrow in his heart and discomfort in his stomach, Pedro Recio having convinced him that light, delicate food sharpened the wits, and that this was exactly what mattered most for people placed in command and in positions of responsibility, where they must call not only on the powers of the body but on those of the mind as well.

By this piece of sophistry Sancho was made to put up with hunger — hunger so sharp that in his heart he cursed the governorship, and even the man who had given it to him. Still, hungry as he was, preserve and all, he set about delivering judgments that day, and the first matter that came before him was a question put to him by a stranger, in the presence of the majordomo and the other attendants. It ran like this: “Señor, a wide river divided two districts of one and the same lordship — and will your worship please pay close attention, because the case is an important one and rather tangled. Now, over this river there stood a bridge, and at one end of it a gallows and a kind of courthouse, where four judges usually sat to administer the law laid down by the lord of the river, the bridge, and the lordship, which ran as follows: ‘Anyone who crosses this bridge from one side to the other must first declare on oath where he is going and on what business. If he swears truly, he shall be allowed to pass; if he swears falsely, he shall die for it, hanged on the gallows standing there, without any reprieve.’ Although the law and its harsh penalty were well known, many people still crossed, and since it was plain at once from their declarations that they were telling the truth, the judges let them pass freely. But it happened that one man, when they came to take his statement, swore by the oath he was taking that he was going to die on that gallows standing there — that and nothing else. The judges deliberated over the oath and said, ‘If we let this man pass freely, he has sworn falsely, and by the law he ought to die; but if we hang him, then since he swore he was going to die on that gallows, he swore the truth, and by the same law he ought to go free.’ Your worship is asked, señor governor: what are the judges to do with this man? They remain in doubt and perplexity to this hour; and having heard of your worship's sharp and lofty intellect, they have sent me to beg your worship, on their behalf, to give your opinion on this intricate and baffling case.”

To this Sancho replied, “Honestly, those gentlemen the judges who sent you to me could have spared themselves the trouble, for there's more of the blunt than the sharp about me; but lay the case out for me once more, so that I can take it in, and then maybe I'll manage to hit the mark.”

The questioner repeated what he had said, once and then again, and at last Sancho said, “The way I see it, I can settle this business in a moment, and here's how: the man swears he is going to die on the gallows; now if he does die on it, he swore the truth, and by the law as enacted he deserves to go free and cross the bridge; but if they don't hang him, then he swore falsely, and by that same law he deserves to be hanged.”
“It is exactly as the señor governor says,” said the messenger; “and as far as a complete grasp of the case goes, there is nothing more to wish for or to question.”
“Well then, here's what I say,” said Sancho: “let the part of this man that swore truly pass over, and hang the part of him that lied; that way the terms of the crossing will be met to the letter.”

“But señor governor,” the questioner replied, “that would mean dividing the man into two parts; and if he is divided, naturally he will die; and then nothing the law requires gets carried out at all — and the law absolutely must be complied with.”

“Look here, my good sir,” said Sancho, “either I'm a blockhead, or there's exactly as much reason for this traveller to die as for him to live and cross the bridge; for if the truth saves him, the lie condemns him in equal measure. And that being so, my view is that you should tell the gentlemen who sent you that, since the arguments for condemning him and the arguments for acquitting him weigh out exactly even, they should let him pass freely, because doing good is always more praiseworthy than doing harm. I'd put my name to that if I knew how to sign; and what I've said here didn't come out of my own head — it's one of the many pieces of advice my master Don Quixote gave me the night before I left to come and govern this island, and it came back to me just now: that whenever the justice of a case is in doubt, I should lean toward mercy. And it's God's will that I remembered it, because it fits this case as if it had been cut to measure.”

“True enough,” said the majordomo; “and for my part I hold that Lycurgus himself, who gave the Lacedemonians their laws, could not have handed down a better ruling than the great Panza has given. Let this morning's session close here, and I will see to it that the señor governor dines entirely to his taste.”
“That's all I'm asking for — fair dealing,” said Sancho. “Give me my dinner, and then let cases and questions rain down on me, and I'll dispatch them in the blink of an eye.”

The majordomo was as good as his word, for his conscience would not let him starve so wise a governor to death — all the more because he meant to be done with him that very night, playing off the last joke he had been commissioned to carry out against him.

So it happened that after Sancho had dined that day — in defiance of all the rules and aphorisms of Doctor Tirteafuera — a courier arrived, just as the cloth was being cleared, bringing a letter from Don Quixote for the governor. Sancho told the secretary to read it through to himself first, and, if there was nothing in it that called for secrecy, to read it out loud. The secretary did so, and after skimming the contents he said, “It may certainly be read aloud, for what Señor Don Quixote writes to your worship deserves to be printed, or set down in letters of gold. It runs as follows.”
A LETTER FROM DON QUIXOTE OF LA MANCHA TO SANCHO PANZA, GOVERNOR OF THE ISLAND OF BARATARIA.

Just when I was expecting to hear reports of your foolishness and blunders, Sancho my friend, I have received news of your good sense instead, for which I give particular thanks to heaven, which can raise the poor man up from the dunghill and make wise men out of fools. They tell me that you govern as if you were a man, and that you are a man as if you were a beast, so great is the humility with which you conduct yourself. But I want you to bear in mind, Sancho, that it is often fitting and necessary, for the authority of the office, to act against the humility of the heart; for a man invested with serious duties should present himself as those duties demand, and not according to what his own modest tastes incline him to. Dress well: a stick dressed up no longer looks like a stick. I do not mean that you should wear jewels or fine clothes, or that being a judge you should dress like a soldier, but that you should wear the apparel your office calls for, and that it should be neat and well turned out. To win the goodwill of the people you govern, there are two things, among others, you must do: one is to be courteous to everyone (though I have told you this before), and the other is to make sure food is plentiful, for nothing grieves the hearts of the poor more than hunger and high prices. Do not issue many proclamations; but those you do issue, see that they are good ones, and above all that they are observed and enforced; for proclamations that are not observed might as well not exist — worse, they spread the idea that the prince who had the wisdom and authority to make them lacked the power to enforce them; and laws that threaten but are never carried out end up like the log that was king of the frogs, which frightened them at first but which in time they came to despise and climb upon. Be a father to virtue and a stepfather to vice. Do not be always strict, nor always lenient; hold to a middle course between those two extremes, for there lies the whole point of wisdom. Visit the jails, the slaughterhouses, and the marketplaces; the governor's presence counts for a great deal in such places: it comforts the prisoners, who hope for a speedy release; it is the dread of the butchers, who for once must give honest weight; and it strikes the same fear into the market-women, for the same reason. Do not let it be seen that you are greedy, a chaser of women, or a glutton — even if by chance you are, which I do not believe — for once the people, and those who have dealings with you, discover your particular weakness, they will train all their batteries on that one spot until they have brought you down to the depths of ruin. Look over and look over again, study and restudy, the advice and instructions I gave you before you left here for your government, and you will see that in them, if you follow them, you have ready at hand a help that will lighten the troubles and difficulties that beset governors at every step. Write to your lord and lady and show yourself grateful to them, for ingratitude is the daughter of pride and one of the greatest sins we know of; and a man who is grateful to those who have done him good shows that he will be grateful to God as well, who has given him so many blessings and goes on giving them. My lady the duchess has sent a messenger off with your suit of clothes and another present for your wife Teresa Panza; we expect her answer at any moment. I have been a little out of sorts from a certain scratching that came my way, not greatly to the benefit of my nose; but it was nothing; for if there are enchanters who mistreat me, there are others who defend me. Let me know whether the majordomo who is with you had any hand in the Trifaldi business, as you suspected; and keep me informed of everything that happens to you, since the distance is so short — all the more because I am thinking of giving up, very soon, this idle life I now lead, for I was not born for it. Something has come up which I rather think will put me out of favour with the duke and duchess; but though I am sorry about it, I do not let it trouble me, for in the end I must answer to my calling rather than to their pleasure, in keeping with the common saying, _amicus Plato, sed magis amica veritas_. I quote you this Latin because I assume that since you became a governor you will have learned it. Farewell; and God keep you from becoming an object of anyone's pity.
Your friend, DON QUIXOTE OF LA MANCHA.

Sancho listened to the letter with close attention, and everyone who heard it praised it and pronounced it wise. He then rose from the table, called his secretary, and shut himself up with him in his own room; and without putting it off a moment longer he set about answering his master Don Quixote there and then, telling the secretary to write down exactly what he dictated, neither adding nor leaving out a thing. The secretary did so, and the reply ran to the following effect.
A LETTER FROM SANCHO PANZA TO DON QUIXOTE OF LA MANCHA.

The press of business on me is so heavy that I have no time to scratch my head or even to cut my nails, which have grown so long — God send a remedy for it. I tell you this, master of my soul, so that you won't be surprised that I haven't written until now to say how I'm faring, well or badly, in this government, where I'm going hungrier than when the two of us were wandering through the woods and the wilds. My lord the duke wrote to me the other day warning me that certain spies had slipped into this island to kill me; so far the only one I've discovered is a certain doctor, hired on a salary in this town to kill every governor who comes here. He's called Doctor Pedro Recio and he comes from Tirteafuera — so you see what a name he has, enough to make a man dread dying at his hands. This doctor says of himself that he doesn't cure illnesses when they turn up, but heads them off before they arrive, and the medicines he uses are diet and more diet, until he's worn a man down to bare bones — as if being skin and bone weren't worse than a fever. In short, he's killing me with hunger, and I'm dying of sheer vexation; for when I thought I was coming to this government to eat my food hot and drink my drink cool, and to take my ease between holland sheets on featherbeds, I find I've come instead to do penance like a hermit; and since I don't do it willingly, I suspect the devil will carry me off in the end. So far I haven't handled any fees or taken any bribes, and I can't think what to make of it; for they tell me here that the governors who come to this island usually have plenty of money either given or lent to them by the people of the town before they ever set foot in it, and that this is the standard custom not only here but with everyone who takes up a government. Last night while making the rounds I came across a beautiful girl in men's clothes, and a brother of hers dressed as a woman. My head-carver has fallen in love with the girl and has picked her out in his own mind for a wife, or so he says, and I've picked the young man for a son-in-law. Today the two of us are going to lay our intentions before the father of the pair, one Diego de la Llana, a gentleman and an old Christian as much as anyone could wish. I've been visiting the marketplaces, as your worship advises me to, and yesterday I caught a stallholder selling fresh hazelnuts and proved she had mixed a bushel of old, empty, rotten nuts in with a bushel of new ones. I confiscated the whole lot for the children of the charity school, who will know well enough how to tell them apart, and I sentenced her to stay out of the marketplace for a fortnight. People told me I handled it bravely. What I can tell your worship is that it's common talk in this town that there's no breed worse than the market-women, for they're all brazen, without conscience, and insolent, and from what I've seen of them in other towns I can well believe it. I'm very glad my lady the duchess has written to my wife Teresa Panza and sent her the present your worship mentions; I'll do my best to show myself grateful when the time comes; kiss her hands for me, and tell her from me that she hasn't thrown her kindness into a sack with a hole in it, as she'll see in the end. I wouldn't want your worship to have any falling-out with my lord and lady; for if you quarrel with them, it's plain the harm must land on me; and since you advise me to be grateful, it won't do for your worship to fail in gratitude yourself toward people who have shown you such kindness and treated you so hospitably in their castle. That business about the scratching I don't understand, but I suppose it must be one of the bad turns the wicked enchanters are forever doing your worship; I'll hear all about it when we meet. I wish I could send your worship something, but I don't know what it would be, unless it's some of the very curious clyster pipes they make on this island, worked with bladders; though if the office stays with me, I'll find something to send one way or another. If my wife Teresa Panza writes to me, pay the postage and forward the letter, for I'm longing to hear how my house and my wife and children are getting on. And with that, may God deliver your worship from ill-meaning enchanters, and bring me well and peacefully out of this government — which I doubt, for from the way Doctor Pedro Recio treats me, I expect to take leave of it and of my life together.
Your worship's servant, SANCHO PANZA THE GOVERNOR.

The secretary sealed the letter and sent the courier off at once; and the men carrying on the joke against Sancho put their heads together and arranged how he was to be packed off from the government. Sancho spent that afternoon drawing up a number of ordinances for the good running of what he took to be the island. He decreed that there were to be no hucksters of provisions in the State, and that wine might be imported from anywhere at all, provided its place of origin was declared, so that a price could be set on it according to its quality, its reputation, and the regard in which it was held; and anyone who watered his wine or changed its name was to forfeit his life for it. He lowered the prices of every kind of shoes, boots, and stockings — shoes above all, since their prices struck him as running extravagantly high. He fixed a set rate for servants' wages, which were galloping unchecked toward the exorbitant. He laid extremely heavy penalties on anyone who sang lewd or loose songs, whether by day or by night. He ordered that no blind man should sing verses about any miracle unless he could produce authentic proof that it was true, since it was his opinion that most of the miracles blind men sing about are trumped up, to the discredit of the real ones. He created and established an alguacil of the poor — not to harass them, but to examine them and find out whether they were genuinely poor; for under cover of a faked crippled limb or a counterfeit sore go many a sturdy thief and drunkard. In a word, he made so many good rules that they are preserved in that place to this day, under the name of _The constitutions of the great governor Sancho Panza_.

title: Part 2, Chapter 52
paragraphs: Which relates the adventure of the second distressed or afflicted duenna, otherwise known as Doña Rodriguez

Cide Hamete tells us that Don Quixote, now healed of his scratches, decided that the life he was living in the castle ran completely against the order of chivalry he professed, so he resolved to ask the duke and duchess for permission to leave for Saragossa, since the festival there was approaching and he hoped to win the suit of armor that is awarded as the prize at tournaments of that kind. But one day, while he sat at table with the duke and duchess and was on the point of acting on his resolution and asking their leave, suddenly there came through the door of the great hall two women — for so they later proved to be — dressed in mourning from head to foot. One of them came up to Don Quixote and threw herself full length at his feet, pressing her lips against them and letting out moans so sad, so deep, and so mournful that everyone who heard and saw her was left bewildered. The duke and duchess assumed it must be some prank their servants were playing on Don Quixote, yet the earnestness with which the woman sighed, moaned, and wept perplexed them and left them in doubt, until Don Quixote, moved by pity, lifted her up and asked her to unveil herself and draw the mantle away from her tear-stained face. She did so, and revealed something nobody could possibly have expected, for she uncovered the face of Doña Rodriguez, the duenna of the household; the other woman in mourning was her daughter, the girl who had been deceived by the rich farmer's son. Everyone who knew her was astonished, and the duke and duchess most of all, for though they considered her a simpleton and a feeble creature, they had never believed her capable of such mad escapades. At last Doña Rodriguez turned to her master and mistress and said to them, "Would your excellences kindly allow me to speak with this gentleman for a moment? I must do so if I am to come out successfully from a business into which the insolence of an ill-intentioned peasant has dragged me."
The duke replied that for his part she had his permission, and that she could talk with Señor Don Quixote as long as she pleased.

Then, turning toward Don Quixote and speaking directly to him, she said, "Some days ago, valiant knight, I told you about the wrong and the treachery a wicked farmer has done to my dearly beloved daughter — the unfortunate girl standing here before you — and you promised me to take up her cause and set right the injury done to her.
