But now word has reached me that you mean to leave this castle in search of whatever good adventures God may grant you; and so, before you set out on the road, I ask that you challenge this insolent rustic and force him to marry my daughter, in keeping with the promise he made to be her husband before he seduced her. To expect my lord the duke to give me justice is to ask the elm tree for pears, for the reason I explained to your worship in private. And with that, may our Lord grant you good health and never abandon us."

Don Quixote answered these words with great gravity and solemnity: "Worthy duenna, hold back your tears — or rather, dry them — and save your sighs, for I take it upon myself to win redress for your daughter, though it would have gone better for her had she not been so quick to trust lovers' promises, which are mostly made in a moment and kept very slowly. So, with my lord the duke's permission, I will set out at once to find this heartless young man, and I will track him down and challenge him and kill him if he refuses to keep his pledged word; for the chief purpose of my profession is to spare the humble and punish the proud — I mean, to aid the distressed and crush the oppressors."

"There is no need," said the duke, "for your worship to go to the trouble of hunting down the rustic this good duenna complains of, nor is there any need to ask my permission to challenge him; for I declare him duly challenged, and I will see to it that he is told of the challenge, that he accepts it, and that he comes to answer it in person here at this castle of mine, where I will provide a fair field for both of you, observing all the conditions that are customarily and rightly observed in trials of this kind, and dealing justly with both sides, as every prince who grants combatants a free field within the bounds of his domain is obliged to do."

"Then with that assurance, and with your highness's kind permission," said Don Quixote, "I hereby, for this occasion, renounce my privilege of gentle birth and lower myself to the level of the offender's humble station, making myself his equal and so entitling him to meet me in combat. And therefore I challenge and defy him, absent though he is, on the grounds of the wrong he did in breaking faith with this poor damsel, who was a maiden and through his misdeed is one no longer; and I declare that he must keep the promise he gave to become her lawful husband, or else stake his life on the issue."

Then, pulling off a glove, he flung it down in the middle of the hall, and the duke picked it up, repeating what he had said before — that he accepted the challenge in his vassal's name. He set the date six days from then, the castle courtyard as the place, and for weapons the usual arms of knights: lance and shield and full armor, with all the rest of the equipment, free of trickery, fraud, or charms of any kind, and inspected and approved by the judges of the field. "But first of all," he said, "this worthy duenna and this unworthy damsel must place their claim for justice in the hands of Don Quixote; otherwise nothing can proceed, and the challenge cannot be carried to a lawful conclusion."
"I do so place it," the duenna replied.
"And so do I," added her daughter, weeping and overcome with shame and confusion.

Once this declaration had been made, and the duke had settled in his own mind how he would handle the affair, the women in black withdrew, and the duchess gave orders that from then on they were not to be treated as servants of hers but as lady adventurers who had come to her house seeking justice. So they were given a room of their own and waited on as though they were strangers, to the alarm of the other women-servants, who could not imagine where the foolishness and recklessness of Doña Rodriguez and her unlucky daughter would end.

And now, to round off the celebration and bring the dinner to a happy close, who should walk into the hall but the page who had carried the letters and presents to Teresa Panza, wife of the governor Sancho. The duke and duchess were delighted to see him, eager to hear how his journey had gone; but when they asked him, the page answered that he could not report it in front of so many people or in a few words, and he begged their excellences to let it wait for a private moment and to entertain themselves with these letters in the meantime; and taking out the letters, he placed them in the duchess's hands. One bore as its address, _Letter for my lady the Duchess So-and-so, of I don't know where_; the other, _To my husband Sancho Panza, governor of the island of Barataria, whom God prosper longer than me_. The duchess's bread would not bake, as the saying goes, until she had read her letter; and after glancing over it herself and seeing it was fit to be read aloud for the duke and everyone present to hear, she read out as follows.
TERESA PANZA'S LETTER TO THE DUCHESS.

The letter your highness wrote me, my lady, gave me great pleasure, for truly it was very welcome. The string of coral beads is very fine, and my husband's hunting suit is every bit its match. The whole village is delighted that your ladyship has made my good man Sancho a governor, though nobody will believe it — least of all the curate, and Master Nicholas the barber, and the bachelor Samson Carrasco; but I don't mind that, for as long as it's true, which it is, they can all say whatever they please. Though to be honest, if the coral beads and the suit hadn't arrived, I wouldn't have believed it either; for everyone in this village takes my husband for a blockhead, and apart from governing a herd of goats they can't imagine what sort of government he could be fit for. God grant it, and guide him as he sees his children have need. With your worship's leave, lady of my soul, I've made up my mind to make the most of this fine day and go to Court, to stretch out at my ease in a coach and make all those who already envy me burst their eyes out. So I beg your excellence to order my husband to send me a small trifle of money — and let it be enough to mention — because expenses run high at Court: a loaf costs a real, and meat is thirty maravedis a pound, which is past all bearing. And if he doesn't want me to go, let him tell me in good time, for my feet are itching to be off; and my friends and neighbors tell me that if my daughter and I cut a fine figure and make a brave show at Court, my husband will come to be known through me far more than I through him, for naturally plenty of people will ask, "Who are those ladies in that coach?" and some servant of mine will answer, "The wife and daughter of Sancho Panza, governor of the island of Barataria;" and that way Sancho will become known, and I'll be well thought of, and "to Rome for everything." I am as annoyed as can be that no acorns were gathered in our village this year; even so I'm sending your highness about half a peck of them, which I went to the wood to gather and picked out one by one myself, and I couldn't find any bigger; I wish they were the size of ostrich eggs. Don't let your high mightiness forget to write to me, and I'll be sure to answer and tell you how I am and whatever news there is in this place, where I remain, praying our Lord to keep your highness in his care and not to forget me. Sancha my daughter and my son kiss your worship's hands. She who would rather see your ladyship than write to you,
Your humble servant, TERESA PANZA.

Everyone was greatly entertained by Teresa Panza's letter, especially the duke and duchess; and the duchess asked Don Quixote whether, in his opinion, they might open the letter addressed to the governor, which she suspected must be excellent. Don Quixote said that to please them he would open it himself, and he did so, and found that it read as follows.
TERESA PANZA'S LETTER TO HER HUSBAND SANCHO PANZA.

I received thy letter, Sancho of my soul, and I promise thee and swear as a Catholic Christian that I came within two fingers' breadth of going mad, I was so happy. Believe me, brother, when I heard that thou wert a governor I thought I'd drop down dead from sheer joy — and thou knowest the saying that sudden joy can kill as surely as great sorrow; as for Sanchica thy daughter, she wet herself from pure happiness. There I stood with the suit thou hadst sent me before me, and my lady the duchess's coral beads around my neck, and the letters in my hands, with the man who brought them standing right there, and even so I truly believed and thought that everything I was seeing and touching was a dream; for who could have imagined that a goatherd would end up governor of islands? Thou knowest, my friend, what my mother used to say: one must live long to see much. I say it because I expect to see more if I live longer, for I don't mean to stop until I see thee a tax-farmer or a collector of revenue — offices where, though the devil carries off those who abuse them, the holders always make and handle money. My lady the duchess will tell thee how much I long to go to Court; think it over and let me know thy pleasure; I'll try to do thee credit by traveling in a coach. Neither the curate, nor the barber, nor the bachelor, nor even the sacristan can believe thou art a governor; they say the whole business is a delusion or some enchantment affair, like everything to do with thy master Don Quixote; and Samson says he means to go and find thee and drive the government out of thy head and the madness out of Don Quixote's skull. I just laugh and look at my string of beads and plan the dress I'm going to make for our daughter out of thy suit. I sent some acorns to my lady the duchess; I wish they had been gold. Send me a few strings of pearls, if they're in fashion on that island. Here is the village news: La Berrueca has married her daughter to a good-for-nothing painter who came here to paint whatever turned up. The council hired him to paint his Majesty's arms over the door of the town hall; he asked two ducats, which they paid him in advance; he worked for eight days, and at the end of them had painted nothing, and then said he had no knack for painting such trifles. He gave back the money, yet for all that he has married on the strength of being a good craftsman — though it's true he has now put down his paintbrush and taken up a spade, and goes out to the fields like a gentleman. Pedro Lobo's son has taken first orders and the tonsure, meaning to become a priest. Minguilla, Mingo Silvato's granddaughter, found out about it and has gone to law with him, claiming he promised to marry her. Wicked tongues say she is carrying his child, but he flatly denies it. There are no olives this year, and there isn't a drop of vinegar to be found in the whole village. A company of soldiers passed through; when they left they took three of the village girls with them. I won't tell thee who they are; perhaps they'll come back, and there are sure to be men who'll take them as wives, blemishes and all, for better or worse. Sanchica is making bonelace; she clears eight maravedis a day, which she drops into a moneybox toward setting up house; but now that she's a governor's daughter, thou wilt give her a dowry without her having to work for it. The fountain in the plaza has run dry. Lightning struck the gibbet — and may every bolt land there, for all I care. I'll be waiting for an answer to this, and for thy decision about my going to Court; and so, may God keep thee longer than me, or as long, for I would not want to leave thee in this world without me.
Your wife, TERESA PANZA.

The letters were applauded, laughed over, savored, and admired; and then, as if to set the seal on the whole business, the courier arrived carrying the letter Sancho had sent to Don Quixote. This too was read aloud, and it cast some doubt on the governor's supposed simplicity. The duchess withdrew to hear from the page what had happened to him in Sancho's village, and he told her everything at full length without leaving out a single detail. He gave her the acorns, along with a cheese Teresa had sent as being especially good — better than the cheeses of Tronchon. The duchess received it with the greatest delight, and there we shall leave her, in order to describe how the government of the great Sancho Panza, flower and mirror of all governors of islands, came to its end.

title: Part 2, Chapter 53
paragraphs: Of the troubled end and conclusion that Sancho Panza’s government came to

To imagine that anything in this life will stay forever in the same state is an idle dream; on the contrary, everything here seems to move in a circle — round and round, I mean. Spring gives way to summer, summer to the fall, the fall to autumn, autumn to winter, and winter to spring again, and so time keeps turning on its never-resting wheel. Only human life, swifter than time itself, races toward its end with no hope of renewal, except in that other life which has no limit and no boundary. So says Cide Hamete, the Mohammedan philosopher; for there are many who, by the light of nature alone and without the light of faith, have grasped the fleetingness and instability of this present life and the endless duration of the eternal life we hope for. But our author is speaking here of the speed with which Sancho’s government ended, melted away, disappeared — vanished, as it were, into smoke and shadow. As Sancho lay in bed on the night of the seventh day of his governorship, sated not with bread and wine but with handing down judgments, giving opinions, and issuing laws and proclamations, sleep — in spite of his hunger — was just beginning to close his eyelids when he heard such a din of bell-ringing and shouting that you would have thought the whole island was going under. He sat up in bed and listened intently, trying to work out what could be causing so great an uproar; but not only could he not discover it — when countless drums and trumpets joined the clamor of the bells and shouts, he grew more bewildered than ever, and was filled with fear and dread. Getting up, he put on a pair of slippers because the floor was damp, and without throwing on a dressing gown or anything of the sort he rushed out the door of his room, just in time to see more than twenty people coming along a corridor with lighted torches and drawn swords in their hands, all shouting, “To arms, to arms, señor governor, to arms! The enemy has landed on the island in countless numbers, and we are lost unless your skill and courage come to our rescue.”

Keeping up this noise, commotion, and uproar, they came to where Sancho stood stunned and bewildered by everything he was seeing and hearing, and as they drew near one of them shouted to him, “Arm yourself at once, your lordship, unless you want to be destroyed and the whole island lost with you.”

“What business do I have with arming?” said Sancho. “What do I know about weapons or rescues? Better to leave all that to my master Don Quixote, who will settle it and make everything safe in an instant; for I, sinner that I am, God help me, understand nothing about these brawls.”

“Ah, señor governor,” said another, “what faintheartedness is this! Arm yourself; here are arms for you, offensive and defensive alike; come out to the plaza and be our leader and captain — it falls to you by right, since you are our governor.”

“Arm me, then, in God’s name,” said Sancho, and they immediately produced two large shields they had brought along and strapped them onto him over his shirt, without letting him put on anything else — one shield in front and the other behind — and passing his arms through openings they had cut, they bound him tight with ropes, so that there he stood, walled and boarded in, straight as a spindle, unable to bend his knees or move a single step. They put a lance in his hand, which he leaned on to keep himself from falling, and as soon as they had him rigged out like this they ordered him to march forward, lead them on, and put courage into them all; for with him as their guide, their lamp, and their morning star, they were certain to bring the business to a happy conclusion.

“And how am I supposed to march, unlucky creature that I am,” said Sancho, “when I can’t move my kneecaps, because these boards tied so tight against my body won’t let me? What you’ll have to do is carry me in your arms and lay me across some postern gate, or stand me upright in one, and I’ll hold it either with this lance or with my own body.”

“On with you, señor governor!” cried another. “It’s fear more than the boards that keeps you from moving. Hurry up, get yourself going, for there’s no time to lose; the enemy is growing in numbers, the shouting is getting louder, and the danger is pressing in.”

Spurred on by these urgings and reproaches, the poor governor made an attempt to move forward — and fell to the ground with such a crash that he thought he had smashed himself to pieces. There he lay, like a tortoise shut up inside its shell, or a side of bacon pressed between two kneading-troughs, or a boat turned bottom-up on the beach; and the gang of pranksters felt no pity at all when they saw him fall. Far from it: putting out their torches, they began shouting again and renewing the calls to arms with such fury — trampling over poor Sancho and slashing at him over the shields with their swords — that if he had not pulled himself together, made himself small, and drawn his head in between the shields, things would have gone very badly for the poor governor. Squeezed into that narrow space, he lay there sweating and sweating again, commending himself with all his heart to God to deliver him from this peril. Some stumbled over him, others fell on top of him, and one man actually planted himself on top of him for a good while, and from there, as if from a watchtower, gave orders to the troops, shouting, “Over here, our men! The enemy is thickest here! Hold that breach! Shut that gate! Barricade those ladders! Bring up the stink-pots of pitch and resin, and the kettles of boiling oil! Block the streets with feather beds!” In short, in his zeal he named every little thing, every implement and engine of war used to beat back an assault on a city, while the bruised and battered Sancho, who heard it all and suffered it all, kept saying to himself, “O, if it would only please the Lord to let the island fall this instant, so that I could find myself dead or out of this torment!” Heaven heard his prayer, and when he least expected it he heard voices crying, “Victory, victory! The enemy is beaten and retreating! Come, señor governor — get up, come enjoy the victory and divide the spoils won from the foe by the might of that invincible arm.”

“Lift me up,” said the miserable Sancho in a doleful voice. They helped him to his feet, and once he was standing he said, “The enemy I’ve beaten you can nail to my forehead. I don’t want to divide any spoils of the foe; all I beg and entreat of some friend, if I have one, is a swallow of wine, because I’m parched with thirst — and wipe me dry, because I’m dissolving into water.”

They rubbed him down, brought him wine, and untied the shields, and he sat down on his bed and, what with fear, agitation, and exhaustion, fainted away. The people who had been in on the joke were sorry now that they had pushed it so far; but the alarm his fainting had caused them was eased when he came back to himself. He asked what time it was; they told him day was just breaking. He said nothing more and began to dress in silence, while everyone watched him, waiting to see what this hurry to get his clothes on could mean.

At last he was dressed, and then — slowly, for he was badly bruised and could not move quickly — he made his way to the stable, followed by everyone present. Going up to Dapple, he embraced him, gave him a loving kiss on the forehead, and said, not without tears in his eyes, “Come along, my comrade and friend, partner in my labors and sorrows. When I was with you, and had no cares beyond mending your harness and feeding your little body, my hours, my days, and my years were happy ones; but since I left you and climbed the towers of ambition and pride, a thousand miseries, a thousand troubles, and four thousand anxieties have entered my soul.” And all the while he was talking this way he was strapping the pack-saddle onto the ass, without anyone saying a word. Then, with Dapple saddled, he climbed onto him with great pain and difficulty, and addressing the majordomo, the secretary, the head carver, Pedro Recio the doctor, and several others standing by, he said, “Make way, gentlemen, and let me go back to my old freedom; let me go find my former life, and raise myself up out of this present death. I was not born to be a governor, or to defend islands or cities from whatever enemies choose to attack them. Plowing and digging, dressing and pruning vines, suit me better than defending provinces or kingdoms. Saint Peter is fine in Rome — I mean, each of us is best off at the trade he was born to. A reaping-hook sits better in my hand than a governor’s scepter. I’d rather eat my fill of gazpacho than be at the mercy of a meddling doctor who kills me with hunger; and I’d rather stretch out in summer under the shade of an oak, and wrap myself in winter in a double sheepskin jacket, in freedom, than lie between holland sheets and dress in sables under the burden of a government. God be with your worships, and tell my lord the duke that ‘naked I was born, naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain’ — I mean that I came into this government without a penny and I leave it without a penny, which is very different from how governors usually depart from other islands. Now stand aside and let me go; I have to plaster myself up, because I believe every one of my ribs is crushed, thanks to the enemies who have been walking all over me tonight.”

“There is no need for that, señor governor,” said Doctor Recio, “for I will give your worship a draught against falls and bruises that will soon make you as sound and strong as ever; and as for your diet, I promise your worship to mend my ways and let you eat your fill of whatever you like.”

“You speak too late,” said Sancho. “I’d as soon turn Turk as stay here any longer. These jokes won’t work a second time. By God, I’d no more remain in this government, or accept another one — even if it were served up to me between two plates — than I’d fly to heaven without wings. I’m of the breed of the Panzas, and every one of them is stubborn: once they say ‘odds,’ odds it has to be, even if it turns out evens, no matter what the world says. Here in this stable I leave behind the ant’s wings that carried me up into the air for the swifts and the other birds to eat me; let’s get back to level ground and our own two feet — and if they aren’t shod in fancy pinked shoes of cordovan leather, they won’t lack for rough hempen sandals. ‘Every ewe to her own kind,’ and ‘let no one stretch his leg further than the sheet reaches’; and now let me pass, for it’s getting late for me.”

To this the majordomo replied, “Señor governor, we would let your worship go with all our hearts, though it grieves us deeply to lose you, for your wit and your Christian conduct naturally make us sorry to part with you. But everyone knows that a governor, before leaving the place he has governed, is obliged first of all to render an account. Let your worship give one for the ten days you have held the government, and then go, and the peace of God go with you.”

“No one can demand that of me,” said Sancho, “except whoever my lord the duke appoints; and I’m on my way to see him now, and to him I will render an exact account. Besides, when I leave as naked as I do, no other proof is needed to show that I have governed like an angel.”
“By God, the great Sancho is right,” said Doctor Recio, “and we ought to let him go, for the duke will be delighted beyond measure to see him.”

They all agreed and let him go, first offering to keep him company and to supply him with anything he might want for his own comfort or for the journey. Sancho said he wanted nothing more than a little barley for Dapple and half a cheese and half a loaf of bread for himself; the distance was so short that there was no need for better or more abundant provisions. They all embraced him, and he, in tears, embraced every one of them, and left them marveling not only at his words but at his firm and sensible resolution.

title: Part 2, Chapter 54
paragraphs: Which deals with matters concerning this history and nothing else

The duke and duchess decided that the challenge Don Quixote had issued against their vassal, for the reason already described, should go forward; and since the young man in question was in Flanders, where he had fled to avoid having Doña Rodriguez as a mother-in-law, they arranged to put a Gascon lackey named Tosilos in his place, first coaching him thoroughly in everything he would have to do. Two days later the duke informed Don Quixote that in four days' time his opponent would appear on the field armed as a knight, ready to maintain that the damsel was lying by half a beard—no, by a whole beard—if she claimed he had ever promised to marry her. Don Quixote was delighted by the news; he promised himself he would work wonders in the lists, and counted it a rare stroke of luck that an opportunity had arisen to show his noble hosts just what the strength of his mighty arm could accomplish. So, in high spirits and great contentment, he waited out the four days, which, measured against his impatience, seemed to stretch into four hundred centuries. Let us leave them to pass, as we leave other things, and go keep Sancho company, who, mounted on Dapple, half cheerful and half melancholy, was making his way along the road to rejoin his master, whose company pleased him more than being governor of all the islands in the world. Now it happened that before he had traveled very far from the island of his governorship (whether what he had governed was an island, city, town, or village, he never bothered to find out), he saw coming toward him along his road six pilgrims with staves—foreigners of the kind who beg for alms by singing. As they drew near they formed themselves into a row, and raising their voices all at once they began to sing in their own language something Sancho could not make out, except for a single word that came through clearly: “alms,” from which he gathered that alms were what their song was asking for. Being, as Cide Hamete tells us, exceedingly charitable, he took from his alforjas the half loaf and half cheese he had been supplied with and handed them over, signaling to them that he had nothing else to give. They accepted these very gladly, but cried out, “Geld! Geld!”
“I don't understand what you want from me, good people,” said Sancho.

At that, one of them pulled a purse from inside his shirt and showed it to Sancho, who now understood they were asking for money. Pressing his thumb against his throat and sweeping his open hand upward, he conveyed to them that he didn't have a coin to his name, and spurring Dapple forward, he pushed through them. But as he was passing, one of them, who had been studying him very intently, rushed at him, threw his arms around him, and exclaimed in a loud voice and excellent Spanish, “God bless me! What is this I'm seeing? Can it really be that I'm holding in my arms my dear friend, my good neighbor Sancho Panza? There's no doubt about it—I'm not dreaming, and I'm not drunk at the moment either.”

Sancho was astonished to hear himself called by name and to find himself embraced by a foreign pilgrim, and though he stared at him steadily without saying a word, he still could not place him. Seeing his confusion, the pilgrim cried, “What! Is it possible, Sancho Panza, that you don't recognize your neighbor Ricote, the Morisco shopkeeper from your own village?”

Sancho then looked at him more closely, began to trace the familiar features, and at last knew him perfectly; and without dismounting from his donkey he threw his arms around the man's neck and said, “Who the devil could have recognized you, Ricote, in this carnival outfit you're wearing? Tell me—who turned you into a Frenchman, and how do you dare come back to Spain? If they catch you and recognize you, things will go badly enough for you.”

“If you don't give me away, Sancho,” said the pilgrim, “I'm safe, because no one will recognize me in this dress. But let's get off the road and into that grove over there, where my companions are going to eat and rest. You'll eat with them—they're very good fellows—and I'll have plenty of time then to tell you everything that's happened to me since I left our village, obeying his Majesty's edict that threatened such harsh penalties against the unfortunate people of my nation, as you've heard.”

Sancho agreed, and after Ricote had spoken with the other pilgrims, they withdrew to the grove they had spotted, turning a good distance off the road. They threw down their staves, stripped off their pilgrim cloaks, and stood in their undergarments; all of them were handsome young men except Ricote, who was getting on in years. Every one of them carried alforjas, and all of them apparently well stocked—at least with things that provoke thirst, the kind that could summon it from two leagues away. They stretched out on the ground, and using the grass as a tablecloth they laid out bread, salt, knives, walnuts, scraps of cheese, and ham bones picked clean—too far gone for gnawing but not for sucking. They also set out a black delicacy called, so they say, caviar, made from fish eggs, a mighty waker of thirst. There was no shortage of olives either—dried ones, admittedly, with no seasoning at all, but tasty and pleasant for all that. What made the finest showing on that field of feasting, though, was half a dozen botas of wine, for each man produced his own from his alforjas; even the good Ricote, who had transformed himself from a Morisco into a German or a Dutchman, brought out his, which in size could have rivaled the other five. Then they began to eat with tremendous relish and at a very leisurely pace, savoring each mouthful—taking only tiny bits of everything on the point of the knife—and then, all at the same instant, they raised their arms and their botas into the air, the mouths of the wineskins pressed to their own mouths and every eye fixed on heaven as if they were taking aim at it. They held that posture a good long while, swaying their heads from side to side as if in tribute to the pleasure they were enjoying, while they emptied the entrails of the bottles into their own stomachs.

Sancho watched it all, “and none of it grieved him”; on the contrary, following the proverb he knew so well—when in Rome, do as you see done—he asked Ricote for his bota and took aim like the rest of them, and with no less pleasure. Four times the botas allowed themselves to be hoisted, but the fifth attempt was useless, for by then they were drier and more juiceless than a reed, which made the merriment that had carried them this far start to wilt.

Every so often one of them would clasp Sancho's right hand in his own and say, “Español y Tudesqui tuto uno: bon compaño,” and Sancho would answer, “Bon compaño, jur a Di!” and then break into a fit of laughter that lasted an hour, without sparing a single thought just then for anything that had happened to him in his governorship—for worries hold very little power over us while we are eating and drinking. At last, the wine having run out on them, drowsiness began to settle over them all, and they fell asleep right there on their table and tablecloth. Only Ricote and Sancho stayed awake, since they had eaten more and drunk less; and Ricote, drawing Sancho aside, sat down with him at the foot of a beech tree, leaving the pilgrims buried in sweet sleep. Then, without once slipping into his Morisco tongue, Ricote spoke as follows in pure Castilian:

“You know well, Sancho Panza, my neighbor and friend, how the proclamation or edict his Majesty ordered issued against the people of my nation filled us all with terror and dismay. It certainly did me, so much so that I think the full weight of the penalty had already crushed me and my children before the time allowed us for leaving Spain had even run out. So I decided—wisely, I think, like a man who knows that on a certain date the house he lives in will be taken from him and who looks ahead of time for another to move into—I decided, I say, to leave town by myself, alone and without my family, and go find some place I could move them to comfortably, not in the frantic rush with which the others departed. For I saw very clearly, as did all the older men among us, that those proclamations were not empty threats, as some claimed, but binding laws that would be enforced at the appointed time. And what convinced me of this was what I knew about the vile and reckless schemes our people were nursing—schemes of such a kind that I think it was divine inspiration that moved his Majesty to carry out so bold a resolution. Not that we were all guilty; some among us were true and steadfast Christians. But they were so few that they could not stand against those who were not, and it was not wise to nurse a viper in the bosom by keeping enemies inside the house. In short, it was with just cause that we were punished with banishment—a mild and gentle sentence in some people's eyes, but to us the most terrible that could be inflicted on us. Wherever we are, we weep for Spain; for after all, we were born there, and it is our natural homeland. Nowhere do we find the welcome our miserable condition requires, and in Barbary and everywhere else in Africa, where we expected to be received, helped, and made welcome, that is exactly where they insult us and mistreat us the worst. We never knew our good fortune until we lost it; and the longing nearly all of us feel to return to Spain is so strong that most of those who, like me, know the language—and there are many who do—come back to it, abandoning their wives and children over there, so great is their love for the country. And now I know from experience what they mean by the saying: sweet is the love of one's own land.

“I left our village, as I said, and went to France, and although they received us kindly there, I wanted to see all I could. I crossed into Italy and made my way to Germany, and there it seemed to me we could live with greater freedom, since the people there don't fuss over fine points; everyone lives as he pleases, because in most regions they enjoy liberty of conscience. I took a house in a town near Augsburg, and then I joined up with these pilgrims, who make a habit of coming to Spain in great numbers every year to visit the shrines, which they regard as their Indies—a sure and reliable source of profit. They travel through nearly the whole country, and there isn't a town they don't leave, as the saying goes, stuffed with food and drink and richer by at least a real in cash; and by the end of their travels they come away with more than a hundred crowns saved up, which they convert into gold and smuggle out of the kingdom, either hidden in the hollows of their staves or sewn into the patches of their pilgrim cloaks or by some trick of their own, and carry home to their own country despite the guards at the posts and crossings where they're searched. Now my plan, Sancho, is to retrieve the treasure I left buried—since it lies outside the town, I can do it without risk—and then to write to my daughter and wife, or cross over from Valencia to them, for I know they are in Algiers, and find some way of getting them to a French port and from there to Germany, where we will wait to see what God chooses to do with us. For after all, Sancho, I know for certain that my daughter Ricota and my wife Francisca Ricota are Catholic Christians, and though I am not quite so much of one myself, I am still more Christian than Moor, and I pray to God constantly to open the eyes of my understanding and show me how I am to serve him. But what astonishes me, what I cannot understand, is why my wife and daughter went to Barbary rather than to France, where they could have lived as Christians.”

To this Sancho replied, “Bear in mind, Ricote, that the choice may not have been theirs, because Juan Tiopieyo, your wife's brother, was the one who took them, and being a true Moor he went where the going was easiest for him. And I can tell you something else: I believe you're wasting your trip looking for what you left buried, because we heard that they confiscated a great quantity of pearls and gold coin from your brother-in-law and your wife, which they were trying to get past inspection.”

“That may well be,” said Ricote, “but I know they never touched my hoard, because I never told them where it was, for fear of accidents. So if you'll come with me, Sancho, and help me dig it up and hide it, I'll give you two hundred crowns to ease your needs—and as you know, I know they are many.”

“I would do it,” said Sancho, “but I'm not a greedy man at all. Just this morning I walked away from an office where, if greed had ruled me, I could have made the walls of my house out of gold and been eating off silver plates inside six months. So for that reason, and because I feel I'd be committing treason against my king by helping his enemies, I wouldn't go with you even if instead of promising me two hundred crowns you put four hundred in my hand right now.”
“And what office is this you've given up, Sancho?” asked Ricote.
“I've given up being governor of an island,” said Sancho, “and such an island, I swear, that you won't easily find its equal.”
“And where might this island of yours be?” asked Ricote.
“Where?” said Sancho. “Just two leagues down the road, and it goes by the name of the island of Barataria.”
“Don't talk nonsense, Sancho,” said Ricote. “Islands are out in the sea; there are no islands on the mainland.”

“What do you mean, no islands?” said Sancho. “I'm telling you, friend Ricote, I left it just this morning, and yesterday I was governing there exactly as I pleased, like a sagittarius. But even so I gave it up, because a governor's job struck me as a dangerous line of work.”
“And what did you gain from governing?” asked Ricote.

“What I gained,” said Sancho, “is the knowledge that I'm no good at governing anything, unless maybe a herd of cattle, and that whatever riches come from these governorships are bought at the price of your rest and your sleep—yes, and even your food, because on islands the governors have to eat next to nothing, especially if they have doctors watching over their health.”

“I can't follow you, Sancho,” said Ricote. “It all sounds to me like rubbish you're talking. Who would hand you islands to govern? Is the world running short of men cleverer than you to make governors of? Hold your tongue, Sancho, come back to your senses, and consider whether you'll come with me, as I asked, to help me carry off the treasure I left buried—and treasure really is the word for it, there's so much of it—and I'll give you enough to live on, as I told you.”

“And I've already told you, Ricote, that I won't,” said Sancho. “Be satisfied that I won't betray you, and go your way in God's name and let me go mine. For I know this much: what's honestly earned can be lost, but what's dishonestly gotten is lost along with its owner.”
“I won't press you, Sancho,” said Ricote. “But tell me—were you in our village when my wife and my daughter and my brother-in-law left it?”

“I was indeed,” said Sancho, “and I can tell you that your daughter left looking so beautiful that the whole village turned out to watch her go, and everyone said she was the loveliest creature on earth. She wept as she went, embracing all her friends and acquaintances and everyone who came out to see her, and she begged them all to commend her to God and Our Lady his mother—and she did it so movingly that it brought tears even to my eyes, and I'm not usually one for crying. And believe me, plenty of people would have liked to hide her away, or ride out and carry her off on the road; but fear of going against the king's command held them back. The one who seemed most stricken was Don Pedro Gregorio, that rich young heir you know of, who they say was deeply in love with her; and since she left, he hasn't been seen in our village again, and we all suspect he's gone after her to steal her away—but so far nothing has been heard of it.”

“I always suspected that gentleman had a passion for my daughter,” said Ricote, “but since I trusted my Ricota's virtue completely, knowing he loved her never troubled me. You must have heard it said, Sancho, that Morisco women seldom or never get entangled in love affairs with old Christians; and my daughter, who I believe cared more about being a Christian than about romance, wouldn't have given any thought to the attentions of this heir.”
“God grant it,” said Sancho, “because it would be a sorry business for both of them. But now let me be on my way, friend Ricote, for I want to reach my master Don Quixote tonight.”

“God go with you, brother Sancho,” said Ricote. “My companions are beginning to stir, and it's time for us to be moving on as well.” Then the two of them embraced, Sancho mounted Dapple, Ricote leaned on his staff, and so they parted.

title: Part 2, Chapter 55
paragraphs: What happened to Sancho on the road, and other things that cannot be surpassed

His long delay with Ricote kept Sancho from reaching the duke's castle that day, though he was within half a league of it when night, somewhat dark and cloudy, overtook him. As it was summer, that did not trouble him much, and he turned off the road meaning to wait for morning; but his bad luck and hard fate so arranged it that, while he was looking for a comfortable spot, he and Dapple fell into a deep, dark hole among some very old ruined buildings. As he fell he commended himself with all his heart to God, convinced he would not stop until he hit the bottom of the bottomless pit. But it didn't turn out that way: at little more than three times a man's height Dapple struck bottom, and Sancho found himself sitting on him without the slightest hurt or scrape. He felt himself all over and held his breath to check whether he was sound or had a hole punched in him somewhere, and finding himself whole and in perfect health he poured out thanks to God our Lord for the mercy shown him, since he had been sure he was broken into a thousand pieces. He also ran his hands along the walls of the pit to see if he could get out without help, but they were quite smooth and offered no hold anywhere, which distressed him terribly — especially when he heard how piteously and mournfully Dapple was bemoaning himself, and no wonder he complained, nor was it bad temper, for in truth he was in a very poor state. "Alas," said Sancho, "what unexpected disasters happen at every turn to those who live in this miserable world! Who would have said that a man who saw himself yesterday seated on a throne, governor of an island, ordering servants and vassals about, would see himself today buried in a pit without a soul to help him, without servant or vassal to come to his rescue? Here we must perish of hunger, my ass and I, if indeed we don't die first, he of his bruises and injuries, and I of grief and sorrow. At any rate I won't be as lucky as my master Don Quixote of La Mancha, when he went down into the cave of that enchanted Montesinos, where he found people who made more fuss over him than if he had been in his own house — they say he came in for a table laid out and a bed ready made. There he saw fair and pleasant visions, but here I expect I'll see toads and adders. Unlucky wretch that I am, what an end my follies and fancies have come to! They'll dig up my bones out of this, when heaven wills that I'm found, picked clean, white and polished, and my good Dapple's with them, and by that, perhaps, it will be discovered who we are, at least by those who have heard that Sancho Panza never parted from his ass, nor his ass from Sancho Panza. Unlucky wretches, I say again, that our hard fate should not let us die in our own country and among our own people, where if there was no remedy for our misfortune, at least there would be someone to grieve over it and to close our eyes as we passed away! O comrade and friend, how badly have I repaid your faithful service! Forgive me, and beg Fortune, as best you can, to deliver us out of this miserable strait we are both in; and I promise to set a crown of laurel on your head, and make you look like a poet laureate, and give you double feeds."

In this strain Sancho bewailed himself, and his ass listened but never answered a word, such was the distress and anguish the poor beast was in. At last, after a night spent in bitter moaning and lamentation, day came, and by its light Sancho saw it was wholly impossible to climb out of that pit without help, and he fell to bemoaning his fate and shouting loudly to find out if anyone was within hearing; but all his shouting was crying in the wilderness, for there was not a soul anywhere nearby to hear him, and at last he gave himself up for dead. Dapple was lying on his back, and Sancho got him to his feet, which he could barely keep; and then taking a piece of bread out of his saddlebags that had shared their fortunes in the fall, he gave it to the ass, who was not at all sorry to have it, and said to him as if he understood, "With bread all sorrows are less."

Then he noticed on one side of the pit a hole large enough to admit a person if he stooped and squeezed himself small. Sancho went over and crept through, and found it wide and spacious inside, which he was able to see because a ray of sunlight that came through what you might call the roof showed it all plainly. He saw too that it opened out and widened into another spacious cavity; so he made his way back to where the ass was, and with a stone began to pick the clay away from the hole until in a short time he had made room for the beast to pass easily. Then taking him by the halter, he set off through the cavern to see if there was any way out at the other end. He advanced, sometimes in the dark, sometimes without light, but never without fear. "God Almighty help me!" he said to himself; "what is a misadventure to me would make a fine adventure for my master Don Quixote. He would have been sure to take these depths and dungeons for flowery gardens or the palaces of Galiana, and would have counted on emerging from this darkness and confinement into some blooming meadow; but I, unlucky as I am, hopeless and dispirited, expect at every step another pit deeper than the first to open under my feet and swallow me up for good — 'welcome evil, if you come alone.'"

In this way and with these reflections he seemed to himself to have travelled a bit more than half a league when at last he made out a faint glimmer that looked like daylight finding its way in on one side, showing that this road, which seemed to him the road to the other world, led to some opening.

Here Cide Hamete leaves him and returns to Don Quixote, who in high spirits and contentment was looking forward to the day set for the battle he was to fight with the man who had robbed Doña Rodriguez's daughter of her honour, for whom he hoped to obtain satisfaction for the wrong and injury so shamefully done her. So it happened that, having ridden out one morning to practise and exercise what he would have to do in the encounter awaiting him the next day, as he was putting Rocinante through his paces or pressing him to the charge, he brought the horse's hooves so close to a pit that, but for reining him in tightly, there would have been no avoiding a fall into it. He pulled him up without going down, and coming a little closer examined the hole without dismounting; but as he was looking at it he heard loud cries coming from below, and by listening carefully was able to make out that whoever was uttering them was saying, "Hey, up there! is there any Christian who hears me, or any charitable gentleman who will take pity on a sinner buried alive, on a disgoverned, unfortunate governor?"

It struck Don Quixote that it was Sancho Panza's voice he heard, at which he was taken aback and astonished, and raising his own voice as much as he could, he called out, "Who is down there? Who is that complaining?"

"Who should be here, or who should complain," came the answer, "but the forlorn Sancho Panza, for his sins and for his bad luck governor of the island of Barataria, squire-that-was to the famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha?"

When Don Quixote heard this his astonishment was redoubled and his agitation grew greater than ever, for it occurred to him that Sancho must be dead and his soul in torment down there; and carried away by the idea he exclaimed, "I conjure you by everything I as a Catholic Christian can conjure you by, tell me who you are; and if you are a soul in torment, tell me what you would have me do for you, for since my profession is to give aid and succour to those in need in this world, it will extend also to aiding and succouring the distressed of the other world, who cannot help themselves."
"In that case," the voice answered, "your worship who speaks to me must be my master Don Quixote of La Mancha; in fact, from the tone of the voice it is plainly nobody else."

"Don Quixote I am," replied Don Quixote, "he whose profession it is to aid and succour the living and the dead in their needs; therefore tell me who you are, for you are keeping me in suspense — because if you are my squire Sancho Panza, and you are dead, since the devils have not carried you off and by God's mercy you are in purgatory, our holy mother the Roman Catholic Church has intercessory means enough to release you from the pains you are in; and I for my part will plead with her to that end, as far as my resources will allow. Without further delay, then, declare yourself and tell me who you are."

"By all that's good," was the answer, "and by the birth of whomever your worship chooses, I swear, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha, that I am your squire Sancho Panza, and that I've never died in all my life; but that, having given up my government for reasons that would take more time to explain, I fell last night into this pit where I am now, and Dapple is my witness and won't let me lie about it, because here he is with me, what's more."
And that wasn't all: you would have thought the ass understood what Sancho said, because at that very moment he began to bray so loudly that the whole cave rang.

"Splendid testimony!" exclaimed Don Quixote; "I know that bray as well as if I were its mother, and your voice too, my Sancho. Wait while I go to the duke's castle, which is close by, and I'll bring someone to pull you out of this pit your sins no doubt have landed you in."
"Go, your worship," said Sancho, "and come back quickly, for God's sake; I can't stand being buried alive any longer, and I'm dying of fear."

Don Quixote left him and hurried to the castle to tell the duke and duchess what had happened to Sancho, and they were not a little astonished at it; they could easily understand his having fallen, given the confirming fact of a cave that had been there since time immemorial, but they couldn't imagine how he had quit the government without their getting any notice of his coming. To cut it short, they fetched ropes and tackle, as the saying goes, and by dint of many hands and much labour they hauled Dapple and Sancho Panza out of the darkness into the light of day. A student who saw him remarked, "That's the way all bad governors should come out of their governments, as this sinner comes out of the depths of the pit — dead with hunger, pale, and I'd guess without a penny to his name."

Sancho overheard him and said, "It's eight or ten days, brother growler, since I entered upon the government of the island they gave me, and in all that time I never had a bellyful of food, not even for an hour; doctors persecuted me and enemies crushed my bones; nor had I any chance to take bribes or collect taxes; and if that's the case, as it is, I don't think I deserve to come out in this fashion; but 'man proposes and God disposes'; and God knows what is best, and what suits each one best; and 'as the occasion, so the behaviour'; and 'let nobody say "I won't drink of this water"'; and 'where you think there are bacon flitches, there are no pegs to hang them on'; God knows my meaning and that's enough; I say no more, though I could."

"Don't be angry or annoyed at what you hear, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "or there'll never be an end of it; keep a safe conscience and let them say what they like, for trying to stop slanderers' tongues is like trying to put gates on the open plain. If a governor comes out of his government rich, they say he's been a thief; and if he comes out poor, that he's been a fool and a blockhead."
"They'll be pretty sure this time," said Sancho, "to set me down as a fool rather than a thief."

Talking thus, and surrounded by boys and a crowd of people, they reached the castle, where in one of the corridors the duke and duchess stood waiting for them; but Sancho would not go up to see the duke until he had first stabled Dapple, for he said the poor beast had passed a very bad night in his last quarters. Then he went upstairs to see his lord and lady, and kneeling before them said, "Because it was your highnesses' pleasure, and not from any merit of my own, I went to govern your island of Barataria, which 'I entered naked, and naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain.' Whether I have governed well or ill, I have had witnesses who will say what they please. I have answered questions, I have decided cases, and always dying of hunger, for Doctor Pedro Recio of Tirteafuera, the island's and governor's doctor, would have it so. Enemies attacked us by night and put us in a great fix, but the people of the island say they came out safe and victorious by the might of my arm — may God give them as much health as there is truth in what they say. In short, during that time I have weighed the cares and responsibilities of governing, and by my reckoning my shoulders can't bear them, nor are they a load for my loins or arrows for my quiver; and so, before the government threw me over, I preferred to throw the government over; and yesterday morning I left the island as I found it, with the same streets, houses, and roofs it had when I came in. I asked no loan of anyone, nor did I try to fill my pocket; and though I meant to make some useful laws, I made hardly any, since I was afraid they wouldn't be kept; for in that case it comes to the same thing to make them or not to make them. I quit the island, as I said, with no escort except my ass; I fell into a pit, I pressed on through it, until this morning by the light of the sun I saw a way out, but not so easy a one but that, had not heaven sent me my master Don Quixote, I'd have stayed there till the end of the world. So now my lord and lady duke and duchess, here is your governor Sancho Panza, who in the bare ten days he has held the government has come by the knowledge that he wouldn't give anything to be governor, not to say of an island, but of the whole world; and that point being settled, kissing your worships' feet, and imitating the game of the boys when they say, 'jump and give me one,' I take a leap out of the government and pass into the service of my master Don Quixote; for after all, though there I eat my bread in fear and trembling, at least I eat my fill; and for my part, so long as I'm full, it's all the same to me whether it's with carrots or with partridges."

Here Sancho brought his long speech to an end, Don Quixote having been the whole time in dread of his uttering a host of absurdities; and when he found him leave off with so few, he gave heartfelt thanks to heaven. The duke embraced Sancho and told him he was heartily sorry he had given up the government so soon, but that he would see to it he was provided with some other post on his estate less burdensome and more profitable. The duchess also embraced him, and gave orders that he should be taken good care of, for it was plain to see he had been badly treated and worse bruised.

title: Part 2, Chapter 56
paragraphs: The prodigious and unparalleled battle that took place between Don Quixote of La Mancha and the lacquey Tosilos in defence of the daughter of Doña Rodriguez

The duke and duchess had no reason to regret the joke played on Sancho Panza in giving him the government, especially as their majordomo returned the same day and gave them a minute account of nearly every word and deed Sancho uttered or did during the time; and to wind up with, eloquently described the attack on the island and Sancho's fright and departure, all of which amused them a great deal. After this the history goes on to say that the day fixed for the battle arrived, and that the duke, after repeatedly instructing his lacquey Tosilos how to deal with Don Quixote so as to vanquish him without killing or wounding him, gave orders to have the heads removed from the lances, telling Don Quixote that Christian charity, on which he prided himself, could not allow the battle to be fought with so much risk and danger to life, and that he must be content with the offer of a battlefield on his territory (though that was against the decree of the holy Council, which prohibits all challenges of the sort) and not push such an arduous venture to its extreme. Don Quixote bid his excellence arrange every detail of the affair as he pleased, since for his part he would obey him in everything. The dread day having arrived, then, and the duke having ordered a spacious stand to be set up facing the castle courtyard for the judges of the field and the appellant duennas, mother and daughter, vast crowds streamed in from all the villages and hamlets of the neighbourhood to see the novel spectacle of the battle; nobody, dead or alive, in those parts had ever seen or heard of one like it.

The first to enter the field and the lists was the master of ceremonies, who surveyed and paced the whole ground to see that there was nothing unfair and nothing concealed that might make the combatants stumble or fall; then the duennas entered and took their seats, wrapped in mantles that covered their eyes — even their bosoms — and displaying no slight emotion as Don Quixote appeared in the lists. Shortly afterwards, accompanied by several trumpets and mounted on a powerful steed that looked like it would crush the whole place, the great lacquey Tosilos made his appearance on one side of the courtyard with his visor down, stiffly cased in a suit of stout, shining armour. The horse was plainly a Frieslander, broad-backed and flea-bitten, with half a hundredweight of wool hanging from each fetlock. The gallant combatant came well primed by his master the duke as to how he was to behave against the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, warned that he must on no account kill him, but should try to shirk the first encounter to avoid the risk of killing him, as he was sure to do if he met him full tilt. He crossed the courtyard at a walk, and reaching the spot where the duennas were placed stopped to look at the one who demanded him for a husband. The marshal of the field summoned Don Quixote, who had already presented himself in the courtyard, and standing by Tosilos's side he addressed the duennas and asked if they consented that Don Quixote of La Mancha should do battle for their right. They said they did, and that whatever he did on their behalf they declared rightly done, final, and valid. By this time the duke and duchess had taken their places in a gallery overlooking the enclosure, which was packed to overflowing with a multitude eager to see this perilous and unparalleled encounter. The conditions of the combat were that if Don Quixote proved the victor, his opponent was to marry the daughter of Doña Rodriguez; but if he should be vanquished, his opponent was released from the promise that was claimed against him and from all obligation to give satisfaction. The master of ceremonies divided the sun between them and stationed them, each on the spot where he was to stand. The drums beat, the sound of the trumpets filled the air, the earth trembled underfoot, the hearts of the watching crowd were full of suspense, some hoping for a happy outcome, some apprehensive of an untoward ending; and at last Don Quixote, commending himself with all his heart to God our Lord and to the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, stood waiting for the signal for the onset. Our lacquey, however, was thinking of something very different; he was thinking only of what I am now about to tell.

It seems that as he stood contemplating his enemy she struck him as the most beautiful woman he had ever seen in his life; and the little blind boy whom in our streets they commonly call Love had no mind to let slip the chance of triumphing over a lacquey heart and adding it to his trophies. So, stealing gently up on him unseen, he drove a dart two yards long into the poor lacquey's left side and pierced his heart through and through — which he was able to do quite at his ease, for Love is invisible, and comes in and goes out as he likes, without anyone calling him to account for what he does. Well then, when they gave the signal for the onset our lacquey was in an ecstasy, musing on the beauty of her whom he had already made mistress of his liberty, and so he paid no attention to the trumpet, unlike Don Quixote, who was off the instant he heard it and, at the highest speed Rocinante could manage, set off to meet his enemy. His good squire Sancho shouted lustily as he saw him start, "God guide you, cream and flower of knights-errant! God give you the victory, for the right is on your side!" But although Tosilos saw Don Quixote coming at him, he never stirred a step from the spot where he was posted; instead, he called loudly to the marshal of the field, and when the marshal came up to see what he wanted, Tosilos said, "Señor, isn't this battle to decide whether I marry or do not marry that lady?" "Just so," was the answer. "Well then," said the lacquey, "I feel qualms of conscience, and I'd put a heavy burden on it if I went any further with the combat; so I declare that I yield myself vanquished and that I am willing to marry the lady at once."

The marshal of the field was lost in astonishment at Tosilos's words; and as he was one of those who were in on the arrangement of the affair, he didn't know what to say in reply. Don Quixote pulled up in mid-career when he saw that his enemy was not coming on to the attack. The duke couldn't make out why the battle wasn't going on, but the marshal of the field hurried over to let him know what Tosilos had said, and he was amazed and extremely angry at it. Meanwhile Tosilos advanced to where Doña Rodriguez sat and said in a loud voice, "Señora, I am willing to marry your daughter, and I have no wish to obtain by strife and fighting what I can obtain in peace and without any risk to my life."

The valiant Don Quixote heard him and said, "As that is the case I am released and absolved from my promise; let them marry by all means, and as 'God our Lord has given her, may Saint Peter add his blessing.'"

The duke had now come down to the castle courtyard, and going up to Tosilos he said, "Is it true, sir knight, that you yield yourself vanquished, and that out of scruples of conscience you wish to marry this damsel?"
"It is, señor," replied Tosilos.
"And he does well," said Sancho, "for what you have to give to the mouse, give to the cat, and it will save you all the trouble."

Tosilos meanwhile was trying to unlace his helmet, and he begged them to come to his help at once, as he was running short of breath and could not remain so long shut up in that confined space. They removed it in haste, and his lacquey features were revealed to public view. At this sight Doña Rodriguez and her daughter raised a mighty outcry, exclaiming, "This is a trick! This is a trick! They have put Tosilos, my lord the duke's lacquey, on us in place of the real husband. The justice of God and the king against such trickery — not to say roguery!"

"Do not distress yourselves, ladies," said Don Quixote; "this is no trickery or roguery, or if it is, it is not the duke who is at the bottom of it but those wicked enchanters who persecute me, and who, jealous of my reaping the glory of this victory, have turned your husband's features into those of this person, who you say is the duke's lacquey. Take my advice, and despite the malice of my enemies marry him, for beyond a doubt he is the one you want for a husband."

When the duke heard this his anger all but vanished in a fit of laughter, and he said, "The things that happen to Señor Don Quixote are so extraordinary that I am ready to believe this lacquey of mine is not one; but let us adopt this plan and stratagem: let us put off the marriage for, say, a fortnight, and let us keep this person we are uncertain about in close confinement, and perhaps in the course of that time he may return to his original shape; for the spite the enchanters bear Señor Don Quixote can't last so long, especially as it is of so little benefit to them to practise these deceptions and transformations."

"Oh, señor," said Sancho, "those scoundrels are well used to changing whatever concerns my master from one thing into another. A knight he overcame some time back, called the Knight of the Mirrors, they turned into the shape of the bachelor Samson Carrasco of our town and a great friend of ours; and my lady Dulcinea del Toboso they have turned into a common country girl; so I suspect this lacquey will have to live and die a lacquey all the days of his life."

Here Rodriguez's daughter exclaimed, "Whoever this man is who claims me for a wife, I am thankful to him for it, for I'd rather be the lawful wife of a lacquey than the cheated mistress of a gentleman — though the one who played me false was no real gentleman either."

To be brief, all the talk and all that had happened ended in Tosilos being shut up until it was seen how his transformation turned out. All hailed Don Quixote as victor, but the greater number were vexed and disappointed to find that the combatants they had been so anxiously waiting for had not battered one another to pieces — just as boys are disappointed when the man they are waiting to see hanged does not come out because the prosecution or the court has pardoned him. The crowd dispersed, the duke and Don Quixote returned to the castle, Tosilos was locked up, Doña Rodriguez and her daughter remained perfectly contented to see that the affair must end in a marriage one way or another, and Tosilos wanted nothing else.

title: Part 2, Chapter 57
paragraphs: Which tells how Don Quixote took his leave of the duke, and what passed between him and the witty, brazen Altisidora, one of the duchess’s maids

Don Quixote now decided it was time to give up the idle life he was leading in the castle. He imagined that his absence was being sorely felt elsewhere while he let himself stay shut away and inactive among the endless comforts and pleasures his hosts heaped on him as a knight, and he believed, too, that he would one day have to give heaven a strict accounting for all that laziness and seclusion. So one day he asked the duke and duchess for permission to depart. They granted it, while making it plain that they were genuinely sorry to see him go.

The duchess handed Sancho Panza the letters from his wife, and he wept over them, saying, “Who would have guessed that all the grand hopes the news of my governorship stirred up in the breast of my wife Teresa Panza would come down to this — me heading back to the wandering adventures of my master Don Quixote of La Mancha? Still, I’m pleased my Teresa did the proper thing in sending the acorns; if she hadn’t sent them I’d have been hurt, and she’d have looked ungrateful. One comfort is that nobody can call that present a bribe, since I already had the government when she sent it, and it’s only fair that people who’ve had a kindness done them should show some thanks, even if it’s with a small thing. The plain truth is, I went into the government naked and I come out of it naked, so I can say with a clear conscience — and that’s no small thing — ‘naked I was born, naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain.’”

So Sancho talked to himself on the day of their departure, while Don Quixote, who had said his farewells to the duke and duchess the night before, came out early in the morning in full armor into the castle courtyard. The whole household was watching him from the galleries, and the duke and duchess came out to see him off as well. Sancho sat on his Dapple with his saddlebags, his valise, and his provisions, perfectly delighted, because the duke’s majordomo — the same man who had played the part of the Trifaldi — had slipped him a little purse containing two hundred gold crowns to cover the expenses of the road, though Don Quixote as yet knew nothing about it. While everyone, as has been said, stood watching him, the brazen and witty Altisidora suddenly raised her voice from among the duennas and waiting-maids and cried out in mournful tones:

Listen, cruel knight;
pull up your reins — what need is there
to drive your spurs into the flanks
of that badly broken steed?
What is it you are fleeing?
I am no dragon in your way,
not even a sheep,
but a tender young lamb gone astray.
You have jilted a maiden
as lovely to behold
as any nymph of Diana
or the Venus of old.
Bireno, Æneas — what worse name can I call you?
May Barabbas go with you! May every evil befall you!

In your claws, pitiless robber,
you carry off as your prey
the heart of a meek
and loving maid today.
Three kerchiefs you have stolen,
and of garters a pair,
from legs that outshine
the whitest marble anywhere;
and the sighs that pursue you
would burn down to the ground
two thousand cities of Troy,
if that many could be found.
Bireno, Æneas — what worse name can I call you?
May Barabbas go with you! May every evil befall you!

May no drop of mercy
ever be granted to Sancho,
and may your Dulcinea
remain enchanted still;
may your treachery to me
find its punishment in her,
for in my country the righteous
often pay for the sinner.
May your grandest adventures
end in defeat and shame,
may your joys be nothing but dreams,
and your love forgotten like your name.
Bireno, Æneas — what worse name can I call you?
May Barabbas go with you! May every evil befall you!

All the time the unhappy Altisidora was lamenting in this fashion, Don Quixote stood staring at her; then, without a word of reply to her, he turned to Sancho and said, “Sancho, my friend, I implore you by the lives of your ancestors to tell me the truth: have you, by any chance, taken the three kerchiefs and the garters this lovesick maiden is talking about?”
To this Sancho answered, “The three kerchiefs I do have; but as for the garters — they’re as far away as ‘over the hills of Úbeda.’”

The duchess was astonished at Altisidora’s nerve. She knew the girl was bold, lively, and impudent, but not, she thought, to the point of daring a liberty like this; and since no one had warned her of the joke, her amazement was all the greater. The duke, wanting to keep the game going, said, “It strikes me as poorly done, sir knight, that after the hospitality you have enjoyed in this very castle you should have presumed to make off with three kerchiefs at the least, to say nothing of my maid’s garters. It argues a bad heart and sits ill with your reputation. Give back her garters, or else I challenge you to mortal combat — and I am not afraid of any rascally enchanters changing or swapping my face the way they changed the face of the man who fought you into that of my lackey, Tosilos.”

“God forbid,” said Don Quixote, “that I should ever draw my sword against your illustrious person, from whom I have received so many favors. The kerchiefs I will return, since Sancho says he has them; but the garters are out of the question, for I do not have them and neither does he — and if this maid of yours will search her hiding-places, I promise you she will find them there. I have never been a thief, my lord duke, and I never mean to be one as long as I live, provided God does not withdraw his keeping from me. This damsel, by her own admission, speaks as a woman in love, and for that I bear no blame; so I have no pardon to ask, either of her or of your excellence, whom I beg to think better of me, and once again to give me leave to continue my journey.”

“And may God speed it so well, Señor Don Quixote,” said the duchess, “that we may always hear good news of your deeds. Go, and God be with you; for the longer you linger here, the hotter you make the fires in the hearts of the damsels who look at you — and as for this one of mine, I will discipline her so thoroughly that from now on she will not misbehave with her eyes or her tongue.”

“One word more, O valiant Don Quixote, and only one — hear me out,” said Altisidora. “I beg your pardon about the theft of the garters; for by God and on my soul, I am wearing them this minute, and I have made the same blunder as the man who went off hunting for his donkey while he was sitting on its back.”
“What did I tell you?” said Sancho. “A fine one I am to go hiding stolen goods! If I’d wanted any part of that trade, I had chances enough handed to me in my government.”

Don Quixote bowed his head and saluted the duke and duchess and all the onlookers; then, wheeling Rocinante around, with Sancho following on Dapple, he rode out of the castle and set his course for Saragossa.

title: Part 2, Chapter 58
paragraphs: Which tells how adventures came crowding in on Don Quixote so thickly that they gave one another no breathing room

When Don Quixote found himself in open country, free, and delivered from Altisidora's attentions, he felt at ease again, his spirits refreshed for taking up the pursuit of chivalry once more; and turning to Sancho he said, “Freedom, Sancho, is one of the most precious gifts heaven ever gave to men. No treasure the earth holds buried or the sea keeps hidden can equal it. For freedom, as for honor, a man may and should risk his life; and by the same token, captivity is the worst evil that can befall a human being. I say this, Sancho, because you saw the good living, the sheer abundance, we enjoyed in that castle we are now leaving. Well, in the middle of all those delicate banquets and snow-chilled drinks, I felt as if I were suffering the pangs of hunger, because I did not enjoy them with the freedom I would have felt if they had been my own; the sense of being obliged to repay benefits and favors received is a shackle that hobbles the independence of the spirit. Happy the man to whom heaven has given a crust of bread for which he owes thanks to no one but heaven itself!”

“For all your worship says,” Sancho answered, “it would hardly be right for us to show no gratitude for the two hundred gold crowns the duke's majordomo gave me in a little purse, which I carry next to my heart like a warming plaster or a comforter, against whatever may come up; we won't always be finding castles where they entertain us — now and then we'll stumble on roadside inns where they beat us with sticks instead.”

Talking in this vein, the knight-errant and his squire-errant went on with their journey, and when they had traveled a little more than half a league they caught sight of about a dozen men dressed like laborers, stretched out on their cloaks on the grass of a green meadow, eating their midday meal. Near them lay what looked like white sheets covering objects underneath, some standing upright and some flat, spaced out at intervals. Don Quixote rode up to the men eating, and after first greeting them courteously, he asked what it was the cloths were covering. “Señor,” one of the group replied, “under these cloths are some carved relief images meant for a retablo we are setting up in our village. We carry them covered so they won't get dirty, and on our shoulders so they won't get broken.”
“With your kind permission,” said Don Quixote, “I would very much like to see them; images carried with such care must surely be fine ones.”

“I should say they are!” said the man. “Let what they cost tell you that — the plain truth is, there isn't one of them that didn't set us back more than fifty ducats. And so your worship can judge for yourself, wait a moment and you shall see with your own eyes.” Getting up from his meal, he went and uncovered the first image, which turned out to be Saint George on horseback, a serpent coiling at his feet and the lance driven down its throat with all the ferocity these scenes usually show. The whole group was, as the saying goes, one blaze of gold. At the sight of it Don Quixote said, “That knight was one of the finest knights-errant the army of heaven ever had. His name was Don Saint George, and he was, besides, a protector of maidens. Let us see the next one.”

The man uncovered it, and it proved to be Saint Martin on his horse, dividing his cloak with the beggar. The moment Don Quixote saw it he said, “This knight too was one of the Christian adventurers, though I believe he was generous rather than valiant — as you can see, Sancho, from his splitting his cloak with the beggar and giving him half. It must surely have been winter at the time; otherwise, charitable as he was, he would have given him the whole thing.”
“That probably wasn't the reason,” said Sancho. “More likely he went by the proverb that says, ‘It takes brains to know when to give and when to keep.’”

Don Quixote laughed and asked them to lift the next cloth, beneath which appeared the image of the patron saint of the Spains on horseback, his sword bloodstained, riding down Moors and trampling heads beneath him; and when he saw it Don Quixote cried, “Ah, now this is a knight, and one of Christ's own squadrons! He is called Don Saint James the Moorslayer, one of the bravest saints and knights the world ever possessed or heaven holds today.”

Then they raised another cloth, which turned out to cover Saint Paul falling from his horse, with all the details that usually appear in pictures of his conversion. When Don Quixote saw it, done in so lifelike a manner that you would have sworn Christ was speaking and Paul answering, he said, “This man was in his day the greatest enemy the Church of God our Lord possessed, and the greatest defender it will ever have — a knight-errant in life, a steadfast saint in death, a tireless laborer in the Lord's vineyard, a teacher of the Gentiles, whose school was heaven and whose instructor and master was Jesus Christ himself.”

There were no more images, so Don Quixote told them to cover everything up again, and said to the men carrying them, “I take what I have just seen as a happy omen, brothers, for these saints and knights followed the same profession I do — the calling of arms. The only difference between them and me is that they were saints and fought with divine weapons, while I am a sinner and fight with human ones. They won heaven by force of arms, for heaven suffers violence; and I, so far, do not know what I have won by all my sufferings. But if my Dulcinea del Toboso were freed from hers, perhaps, with my fortunes mended and my mind restored to itself, I might set my steps on a better road than the one I am traveling now.”
“May God hear that and sin be deaf,” said Sancho to this.
